item.title: Rams vs Eagles: How to watch on TV, stream, or listen on radio
item.description: L.A. needs a win on the road to square their record
item.content:encoded:
Looking to even the ledger after a 1-2 start to the season, the Los Angeles Rams travel across country to the east coast to do battle with the 2-1 Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday October 5. Kickoff is set for 10 a.m. PDT at Lincoln Financial Field in South Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The fall weather will be much more temperate than a winter date. Although full clouds are expected and a 60 percent chance of rain is forecast, temperatures are expected to be in the mid-60’s with mild wind conditions, 7 to 14 miles per hour.

It was 1937, when the Rams were based in Cleveland that the series with Philly had its origins. The pair have squared off 47 times over that span with the Eagles holding a 26-20-1 advantage and have out-scored L.A. 983 to 961. Since Sean McVay took the Rams reins in 2017, Philadelphia has been the bane of his coaching existence, winning six of the seven matchup’s and the last four in a row.

Both teams have been bitten by the injury bug early and several starters have been ruled out of Sunday’s tilt.

For the Eagles, tight end Dallas Goedert and receiver’s Devonta Smith and Hollywood Brown will be absent from an offense that is in the NFL’s Bottom 10 in scoring and total yards. Defensive starters designated as out are linebacker Zach Baun and safety Marcus Epps.

Tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle), cornerback Jaylen Watson (shoulder), and defensive tackle Aaron Donald (back) won’t play for the Rams, while tight end Colby Parkinson and edge Josaiah Stewart are questionable. Ferguson will join edge Myles Garrett and offensive linemen Justin Dedich and Keagan Trost on the Injured Reserve List, all were expected to be prominent pieces in the 2026 season. L.A. also waived their primary kick returner, Xavier Smith, earlier this week.

item.title: ‘All signs point to Tyson Bagent’ starting for the Chicago Bears
item.description: A recent report tabs Tyson Bagent as the likely starter for the Bears on Sunday, plus we share all the results from our poll questions this week.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson may not be tipping his hand on his starting quarterback this Sunday against the New York Jets, but a Friday night report may have shed some light on the situation. Ian Rapoport, ESPN and NFL Network’s national insider, believes he knows what the Bears are doing.

“My understanding is that Tyson Bagent took the majority of the first-team reps at practice this week,” Rapoport said. “While Ben Johnson has not yet named a starter, the expectation is that the backup quarterback, Tyson Bagent, is the starter on Sunday.”

“We’ll see what the Bears end up doing, but all signs point to Tyson Bagent getting he start this week for Chicago.”

With 59% of the vote, our fans also believe Bagent will get the nod on Sunday against the Jets.

Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook share that sentiment because they only offer a passing-yards prop bet for Bagent, not Case Keenum.

Bagent’s passing-yards over/under is 199.5 (-114). If you think he’ll go over 1.5 passing touchdowns, you can get that at +136, and if you think he’ll be under 1.5 TDs, that’s at -182.

Keenum put up 247 yards last week on Monday night, so if you think Bagent will beat that, FanDuel had an over 250 yards option at +250.

What are your thoughts on the Bagent props? Do you think he’ll go over 2 touchdowns? What about his passing yards? Let us know in the comment section.

We had a couple of other Reacts polls this week at Windy City Gridiron, and there was a national question on the SB Nation main NFL page that may interest Bears fans too.

There was some buzz around a Bagent trade this offseason, and if he plays well on Sunday, that could start up again. I’m sure the Bears have a price they’d consider, but that wouldn’t be a day three pick.

Caleb Williams is an ascending superstar.

Tyson Bagent may have only 4 starts in his NFL career, but he plays with the poise of a much more experienced player, and the Bears gave him a contract extension for a reason. Ben Johnson believes in him, and I’m excited to see him play on Sunday.

Case Keenum is a crafty veteran who has won a game as a starter for seven different franchises, tying Ryan Fitzpatrick for the most ever.

I’ve looked at other QB rooms across the NFL, and from 1-3, I don’t see any better.

Chicago’s strong quarterback room is a big reason 94% of our fans think the Bears are heading in the right direction,

item.title: Chris Jones thinks the arrow is pointing up for Sack Nation
item.description: The CEO said that his companies fortunes are about to turn around in Kansas City.
item.content:encoded:
Star defensive lineman and CEO of Sack Nation, a defensive subsidiary of their parent company, the Kansas City Chiefs, which specializes in security infiltration, spoke to media members Thursday afternoon.

Jones admitted the early returns haven’t been what the company hoped for this fiscal year; so far this season, the Chiefs have accumulated only four sacks. Jones acknowledged that Sack Nation has faced a unique set of circumstances while trying to achieve its ultimate goal: tackling the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage while he still has the ball in his hand.

“We’re close, statistically-wise,” Jones told reporters. “You look at the numbers, the quarterback has been getting rid of the ball [in] 2.3 seconds. I don’t care how good of a pass rusher you are, when they’re throwing the ball that quick, it’s tough for anyone,” Jones explained.

To make matters worse, he added that when the opposition holds onto the ball to take a shot downfield, they keep extra men back to bolster their line and prevent any incursion.

“You got seven, eight men in there protecting,” Jones said. “So, it’s like, the opportunity is going to come. I think don’t waver from what we’ve been doing. We’ve done a lot of good. We put a lot of good on film. I think we stay committed to that and just find ways to get sacks out of it so y’all can stop writing about us in the media.”

The job doesn’t get any easier this week, when Jones and his team take on the Las Vegas Raiders. The Raiders have only allowed five sacks through three games this season and are tied for the NFL lead in passing touchdowns with nine.

Part of the Raiders’ success is also due to their quarterback, Kirk Cousins, getting the ball out of his hands quickly this season. Through Week 3, Cousins has the seventh-fastest time to throw in the NFL in 2026 at 2.58 seconds. The Chiefs will need to get home and pressure Cousins to disrupt his rhythm in the passing game.

Not just because it will help Sack Nation improve its bottom line, but also because the alternative is another week of media stories about Sack Nation underperforming.

“It’ll just give you another week to write about the Chiefs defensive linemen suck and why did you all pay me and George (Karlaftis).”

item.title: Packers film room: What went wrong on the Falcons 55-yard run
item.description: Run defense takes a beating in week 3.
item.content:encoded:
Bijan Robinson’s 55-yarder against the Green Bay Packers in week three was the play that turned the game. It came on first down after a roughing the passer penalty on edge rusher Brenton Cox on third down that would have forced the Falcons to punt and given the Packers another chance to add to their 7-0 lead.

The Packers took a 7-0 lead when Christian Watson came uncovered on a play-action pass with 5:13 left in the first quarter. Penix had also thrown an interception on Atlanta’s opening drive, so the Falcons’ offense looked out of sync.

The drive that included the run nearly stalled too. Atlanta started at its own 15 and picked up a first down on an 8-yard pass to Kyle Pitts and a 6-yard Robinson run, but Lukas Van Ness forced Penix into an intentional grounding penalty that left Atlanta facing third-and-11. That was a likely punt situation, and Green Bay’s defense was winning. Instead, Brenton Cox Jr. was called for unnecessary roughness, which gave the Falcons a first down.

Atlanta capitalized right away. On the very next snap, Robinson broke a 55-yard run to the Green Bay 5. The timing mattered as much as the yardage.

A defense that has just given away a first down on a penalty is often a step slow to reset, and Robinson turned that moment into a huge gain. Going from backed up at the 15 to first-and-goal at the 5 within a couple of plays was the biggest field-position swing of the first half.

The play call from Atlanta was an outside zone run concept to the offense’s left side behind their tight end Charlie Woerner and Drake London in tight to the formation.

The Packers countered the Falcons formation with a 5-2 front and two deep safeties behind it. Playing two deep safeties versus the run is risky but the Packers have been excellent defending the run from two high shells the last couple of seasons and Gannon specializes in it.

In fact, the Packers had it bottled up really well initially. Edgerrin Cooper (No. 56) is the edge setter on this play as the defensive end backdoor slants inside. Cooper is the spill/force player responsible for spilling the ball back inside.

Zaire Franklin (No. 44) is the back side leverage player who’s job it is to clean up any open gap and the run if it spills back inside. On the perimeter, Brandon Cisse (No. 2) is the front side leverage player and secondary force.

As Cooper comes down, Woerner blocks him and pancakes him to the ground. Cooper plays the inside shoulder and leaves Cisse on an island if Robinson bounces outside. Sure enough he does as Franklin moves with Robinson’s movement and flashes color in the gaps.

Cisse dives for the tackle and misses. The rookie did not have a great night. A tackle here would have went for a one or two yard gain.

Poor gap responsibility ultimately doomed the defense on this play.

Robinson later scored on a 3-yard run two plays later, tying the game at 7 with 1:32 left in the first quarter. From there, Atlanta took over. The Falcons scored 27 straight points, turning a 7-0 deficit into a 27-7 lead in the fourth quarter.

The run was also the first sign of how the night would go on the ground. Robinson finished with 194 yards and two touchdowns on 29 carries, one yard short of his career high of 195 set against the Rams in 2025. Green Bay managed almost nothing running the ball by comparison. The Packers ran nine times for just 17 yards.

item.title: Giants vs. Cardinals: Which Arizona team is the real one?
item.description: What can we learn in this week’s ‘5 questions’ segment?
item.content:encoded:
With the New York Giants facing the Arizona Cardinals this week we turn to Seth Cox of SB Nation’s Revenge of the Birds for our weekly ‘5 questions’ segment.

Ed: Which is likely the more realistic version of the Cardinals. The team that lost 31-7 to the Seattle Seahawks or the team that pushed the San Francisco 49ers in a 36-30 loss?

Seth: That is the million dollar question for the Arizona Cardinals. We knew the defense would be an issue, more on that later, but we expected a little more from the offense.

The Cardinals threw the ball 52 times for 280 yards against the Niners. Again, the stats 280 yards and two passing touchdowns are good, but their pass game is basically a really good run game. They are the second-worst team in explosive plays and they almost play not to lose, as opposed to make big plays and put pressure on the opposition.

It also tends to coincide with big deficits, so teams are willing to allow them to beat them with a death by thousand cuts, because it runs so much time and they know their own offense will go in and score immediately.

Ed: The Giants drafted Saquon Barkley No. 2 overall in 2018, and as great as he was there were also mixed feelings about that. How do fans feel about the selection of Jeremiyah Love, and does it look like he will justify being the third overall pick in the draft?

Seth: This is a little hard to explain. I think 95% of fans are positive in the sense that Jeremiyah Love was a blue chip prospect and looks like he will be very good to great in the NFL.

However, I feel like it is 50/50 at best if fans agree with the usage of that pick for that position, when you are looking at maybe the worst defense in the NFL that is not actively trying to tank like the Dolphins.

Arvell Reese, Sonny Styles, heck even Caleb Downs may have helped more in the immediate, but I don’t think that means anyone is overthinking it right now, but they are definitely going to continue to monitor things.

Ed: If you could take one player off the Giants’ roster and put him in Arizona’s lineup, who would it be? Why?

Seth: Well, now that Brian Burns is gone, I think it would be Jermaine Eluemunor. The Cardinals desperately need help at the right tackle position and Eluemunor has not only a claim as the best right tackle in the NFL, but maybe as the best tackle overall. That would help the above problem with the pick of Jeremiyah Love and the lack of explosive offensive plays… right?

Ed: What are your early thoughts on Mike LaFleur as a head coach? Does he look like a guy who could be Arizona’s coach for a while?

Seth: Unfortunately for the Cardinals, LaFleur is on the clock as soon as he starts. The average tenure of a Cardinals head coach since they moved to Arizona is three years. Not many coaches get past that, and the ones that do usually flame out very early into their second contract, if they even start that second contract.

That being said, outside of procedural/pre-snap penalties, LaFleur looks more than capable of being a really good head coach in the NFL. So much so that you feel at times like this could be the coach that bucks the trend of misfortune for the Cardinals head coaches. But they need to clean things up, and then show they can compete within their own division for him to have any real shot as being the long-term answer.

Ed: The Cardinals are a slight favorite. If the Giants are going to win, what would that look like? What weaknesses can the Giants exploit?

Seth: Does your team have a quarterback/running back/offensive talent? If so, then this could be your lucky day, as the Cardinals defense has been mostly bad, and sometimes downright atrocious this season.

Think about this stat from the Cardinals 36-30 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, the Cardinals ran 31 more plays and possessed the ball 17 more minutes than the Niners… and the 49ers outgained them by 72 yards. That is really unfathomable. 

So, if the Cardinals defense doesn’t find a way to slow down what has been an impotent offense of the Giants since the injury to Jaxson Dart, I don’t know how they can stop any team’s offense. And also, I don’t see them stopping the Giants offense. They did okay against the Chargers, but I think with how well the Giants are coached, and how much they can run the ball, something the Cardinals cannot stop, it will be an interesting game. 

Stop the short passes by Jacoby Brissett, make him stand in the pocket and try and push the ball down the field and live with the results.

On offense, hand the ball to Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris and work the play action game. 

If you do all of that, the game will be competitive and the Giants as home dogs may look silly.

Good luck and good health in this one.

item.title: Cleveland Browns: Would they trade this veteran WR? Should they?
item.description: Wide receiver Jerry Jeudy has fallen behind the rookies. Does that make him a potential trade candidate?
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns appear to be on the right track at wide receiver.

After far too many years of bad draft picks (Jamari Thrash, Michael Woods II, Anthony Schwartz, Antonio Callaway, and Brian Robiskie, to name a few) and ill-conceived trades (Odell Beckham Jr.), general manager Andrew Berry appears to have hit on rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston.

Following Thursday night’s win over the Pittsburgh Steelers, Concepcion is tied for the team lead with 17 receptions, while Boston leads with 284 receiving yards. Together, the rookie duo has combined for 37 percent of the team’s receptions and 50 percent of the team’s receiving yards. 

Mix in tight end Harold Fannin Jr. (17 receptions and a team-high three receiving touchdowns), and the contributions from running backs Qunshon Judkins and Raheim Sanders (a combined 25 receptions for 169 yards), and that provides quarterback Deshaun Watson with a nice set of tools in the toolbox to work with.

What’s that? There is one prominent name missing from the list? Oh right, Jerry Jeudy.

The veteran of the group, the 2026 season has been an odd one for Jeudy, who was not targeted at all in the win over Carolina and only once in the victory over Tampa Bay.

It was turning into another quiet night for Jeudy against the Steelers before he pulled in two passes on Cleveland’s game-winning drive in the fourth quarter. Those receptions brought Jeudy’s season total to five catches for 62 yards.

There are a few ways to look at the situation:

  • After posting career highs in receptions (90) and receiving yards (1,229) in 2024, Jeudy dipped to 50 receptions and 602 receiving yards in 2025. His slow start could be a sign that he is in decline.
  • Watson is more focused on distributing the ball to whoever is open, rather than trying to force a pass to one particular player, which means Jeudy’s time will come, as it did in the fourth quarter on Thursday.
  • Boston and Concepcion are simply better options, and the Browns consider Jeudy a role player.

Head coach Todd Monken acknowledged that last point in his comments while crediting Jeudy for being there when the team needed him after the game on Thursday:

“I’m so happy for Jerry. And it probably wasn’t enough for a game ball, but for a guy that really isn’t starting now, he’s a rotational player, that’s so cool for him. And it’s not easy for a veteran player to have young players kind of beat him out, but we needed it in a big time, and that was a big time catch.”

That leads to the question of how much the Browns need Jeudy and whether or not they could look to trade him before the NFL trade deadline on November 10.

ESPN’s Dan Graziano highlighted Jeudy as a trade candidate in his latest column on players who could be on the move in the next few weeks:

Jeudy is still only 27 years old, and he’s signed through 2027. But the Browns’ wide receiver corps has been taken over by rookies, and Jeudy might no longer fit squarely into the plans. He’s owed about $23 million in salary and bonus for 2027, but it’s not guaranteed, so an acquiring team wouldn’t likely be deterred by that.

It is always tricky when people start talking about trades. If Jeudy’s numbers are truly an indication that he is slipping, then why would another team want him? And how much value would the Browns receive for him?

But if the numbers are simply based on Watson having better options and Jeudy is still putting in the work and not complaining, then the Browns are likely better off with him on the roster. Especially since they are only four games into the season and injuries are always a concern.

Plus, as he showed against the Steelers, Jeudy can still make a play when the team needs him. So Berry may be hesitant to shake things up when the team is winning.

What do you think, Browns fans? Would you look for a trade partner for Jeudy, or is he a nice insurance policy to have? Let everyone know in the comments!

item.title: Saints vs. Falcons: QB to QB Matchup
item.description: Tyler Shough will face off against Michael Penix Jr. in game to determine the leader of the division
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints will see their bitter rivals enter the Superdom for a primetime matchup on Monday night as they face off against the Atlanta Falcons. The Falcons have been down on their luck, but they are certainly not lacking talent. Their offense still features some of the best young players in the league, including Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts. However, they just can’t seem to find consistency at the quarterback position.

Throughout the offseason, there was a quarterback battle between Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa. Tua actually won the job while Penix continued to recover from an injury. However, before the first game of the season, Tua suffered an injury of his own. The Falcons then turned to Cooper Rush, who started in Week 1 and 2. With the offense struggling to perform, they turned to their fourth quarterback, Jack Strand, who came in and immediately threw a pick-six against the Panthers.

Finally, last week, the Falcons were able to get Penix back, and the offense showed some life. Penix’s first drive of the season also ended with an interception, but after that, the Falcons were able to surprise a lot of people by defeating the Packers on the road, 35-14.

Penix was Atlanta’s starting quarterback last year but struggled to find a rhythm. This could be the year he takes a step forward. In his lone start of the season, Penix completed 18 of 25 passes (72%) for 256 yards, averaging 10.2 yards per attempt, with one touchdown and one interception.

The good news for the Falcons is that they did not allow a single sack against the Packers last week, and that is something the Saints will need to change.

The focus for the Saints’ defense shouldn’t necessarily be to stop Penix. If anything, it should be to force Penix to be the one who has to beat them.

Bijan Robinson went off against the Packers, rushing for 194 yards and two touchdowns, while Drake London complemented the running game with nine receptions for 194 yards. He also had a long reception of 68 yards. Most of Penix’s passing production came from one receiver, while Robinson accounted for much of the offense’s remaining production.

The Saints will need to generate pressure up the middle. With Penix being a left-handed quarterback, the normal pass-rushing dynamics are flipped a little. His blind side is to his right, so the Saints need to prevent him from stepping up into his throws, especially considering that he isn’t much of a threat to run. Flush him out of the pocket and force him to change his throwing spots.

They will also need to take away his first read, which is usually Drake London. Force the Falcons into third-and-long situations by getting to Robinson on early downs and keeping the offense off schedule.

Last year, the Saints had success against Atlanta and Bijan Robinson’s rushing attack. In two games against the Saints, Brandon Staley’s defense held Robinson to a combined 103 rushing yards and zero touchdowns. So, it’s possible.

Tyler Shough and the Saints’ Offense:

Tyler Shough leads the Saints nto this matchup, and had the fourth quarter against the Raiders not been played, Shough would have been coming off the best game of his young career. But football is a four-quarter sport.

Through the first three games, Shough has 912 passing yards and is completing 68.9% of his passes. He also has eight touchdowns and three interceptions.

The most notable thing about Shough’s stat line is that the games in which he has committed a turnover are the games the Saints have lost.

Start by protecting the football.

The Saints also have to help him in that regard because the pass protection has been very poor. Through the first three games, Shough has been sacked 10 times. That’s not good for the offense, and it’s certainly not good to allow your starting quarterback to continue taking hits like that.

The Saints will need to establish a running game around Shough on Monday night, and that challenge just got harder. Travis Etienne Jr. will miss some time after suffering a hamstring injury against the Raiders which means Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara will become the focal points of the rushing attack.

The Saints also did a great job utilizing their tight ends on Sunday, creating mismatches by incorporating more 12 personnel. Noah Fant and Juwan Johnson both played very well because of it.

And, obviously, get the ball to Chris Olave.

Olave is making a case to be the best receiver in the league right now, and the Saints need to continue featuring him in the offense. Find that Guardian Cap early and often on Monday night.

Finally, encourage Shough to run.

He has good mobility and can make a defense pay when its pass rushers become undisciplined. Encourage him to use his legs and make the defense think twice about sending blitzes. He can get rid of the ball quickly and extend plays with his feet.

The Falcons have been able to generate pressure with just four rushers, so it will be important for Shough to make them pay whenever they decide to send more than that.

The Matchup:

When it comes to this matchup, the Saints have the advantage in talent at the quarterback position, while the Falcons have the advantage in the talent surrounding their quarterback.

This is an important game because it’s a divisional matchup, and the Saints are coming off a loss. They can’t afford to lose games within the division if they want to have a chance at the postseason.

The NFC South isn’t a particularly strong division, so the Saints need to come out and win. To do that, they must make sure they showcase that they have the better quarterback on the field Monday night.

Who do you think has the advantage heading into this matchup, and how do you think this game will turn out?

The Denver Broncos are coming off an historic back-to-back comeback wins where they would overcome two score deficits in both games to climb to 2-1 before heading west to take on the undefeated San Francisco 49ers. They are underdogs and the 49ers look pretty good to start the season. This one will put Denver to the test.

With the heat likely being a big factor in this game, Bo Nix and the offense must do a better job of controlling the clock and sustaining their drives. If they find themselves forcing the defense back out onto after multiple three-and-out’s then this game could get ugly for them quickly.

Game Overview

Denver Broncos vs. San Francisco 49ers
Sunday, October 4, 2026 at 2:25 P.M. Mile High time
Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California
ATS Betting Lines: San Francisco -2.5
Moneyline Odds: Denver +124 / San Francisco -146
Over/Under: 47.5
Note: All odds courtesy of FanDuel Sportsbook.

Broncos Country, ride with us on the SB Nation app!

Follow the action and experience every game alongside a community of passionate Broncos fans.

  • Join the live game-day conversation
  • Enjoy fewer ads
  • Easily jump between communities
  • Comment and post faster

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Collectively, our Mile High Report staff is predicting a narrow Broncos 24-23 victory on the road over the 49ers. Here’s how we predicted the outcome individually:

49ers 27, Broncos 16

This is one of those games where I think the Broncos won’t be able to catch fire late. A combination of the heat, poor starts, and inability to sustain drives will catch Denver sleeping. They will mount a late drive, but the defense is too tired to rally. It’s okay, though. Losing on the road to an NFC team is the “best” kind of loss and the Broncos will bounce-back to win the next two games anyway. 4-2 through the first six games was always my target. – Tim Lynch

Broncos 24, 49ers 20

I think this is going to be a difficult matchup for the Broncos, but I have confidence they can get the job done on the road against the 49ers. The Broncos will have to play much better on offense. That includes starting off hot with a formidable rushing attack. On top of that, Vance Joseph’s defense will have to find a way to slow down Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, and the rest of the 49ers high-powered offense. Time of possession and the turnover battle will be huge. I think Denver finds a way to sneak out their third victory. – Chris Hart

item.title: Uchenna Nwosu named Seahawks game captain vs. former team
item.description: A former Charger headlines the latest group of Seahawk captains.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks will need veteran leadership to right their ship in Week 4 after a loss to the Washington Commanders, at least according to the team’s captains, which were announced on Friday.

Seattle announced that Cooper Kupp, Mike Morris, Nehemiah Pritchett and former Los Angeles Charger Uchenna Nwosu will have the honors of being captains on Sunday. Between the four of them, they represent 26 years of experience in the NFL, though the majority of that stems from Kupp (10) and Nwosu (9).

This is every player’s first selection this season and marks the first time that Pritchett, who is stepping up to replace Riq Woolen at starting cornerback, has been named a captain. Pritchett had an interception in Week 1 and has anchored an injured secondary through three games.

Nwosu being named captain is an obvious choice as he was a second-round pick by the Chargers in 2018 before signing with the Seahawks in 2022. In addition to the bit of gamesmanship, Nwosu has become a fan-favorite in Seattle after he propelled a terrible pass-rush in 2022 and became a key part of the “Dark Side” defense. Not to mention his hit on Drake Maye in the Super Bowl, which led to a game clinching interception.

Kupp, the lone offensive representative, has the second most receiving yards of any Seahawks player. The Eastern Washington alum has proven that he still has juice left to squeeze this season after a decade in the league, recording an immaculate catch in Week 1 and being a reliable target in clutch moments.

Lastly, Morris, who is repping the special teams, returned to the lineup last week against the Commanders. The Seahawks fifth-round pick has been a staple of the team’s defensive line rotation the last two seasons, recording two TFLs and 23 tackles in that time frame.

These four will lead the Seahawks onto the field as they face the winless Chargers at Lumen Field on Sunday at 1:25 p.m.

item.title: Colin Kaepernick suggests the 49ers were tanking with Chip Kelly in 2016
item.description: The former 49ers quarterback was not a fan of how the team was handled in 2016
item.content:encoded:
2016 was a rough time to be a 49ers fan, with the team going 2-14 while dealing with a dysfunctional front office. Former 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick suggests the 49ers didn’t want to win anyway.

Kaepernick’s memoir, “The Perilous Fight,” has been out for a couple of weeks and tells his perspective on growing up and playing both college and professional football.

49ers fans looking for stories from his time as the starting quarterback won’t be disappointed. We’ve talked about his relationship with general manager Trent Baalke and head coach Jim Harbaugh, but Kaepernick also shares his perspective playing for the coaches that followed Harbaugh: Jim Tomsula in 2015, whose regime Kaepernick called “a disaster,” and Chip Kelly in 2016.

Kelly named Blaine Gabbert the starting quarterback over Kaepernick. On the surface, it may have seemed like Gabbert beat Kaepernick for the starting job. In reality, Kaepernick was still rehabbing and returning from injury. There were also reports of injury guarantees on Kaepernick’s contract that he eventually restructured to remove—something many (including Kaepernick) speculate was the real reason he stayed off the field.

That’s all common knowledge; what is interesting is Kaepernick’s take on the 49ers in 2016:

I should add that the Niners didn’t seem interested in winning football games. They appeared to be in full “tank” mode. They were calling Chip Kelly’s first season a “rebuilding” year, but in actuality they had no plan to go get the talent Coach Kelly wanted.

Kaepernick used the wide receiver situation as an example. Saying the 49ers’ No. 1 wideout that year was “the number five or six receiver on a different team.” No names are given, but Jeremy Kerley led the team in catches and yards receiving in 2016. Many may think of Torrey Smith as the “designated” wide receiver. Either way, Kerley’s team-leading 516 yards in receiving that year should tell you just how bad the 49ers were.

“The team didn’t get us another receiver,” Kaepernick wrote. “Despite having the money to do so, something like $40 million in salary cap space.”

Publicly, the 49ers were rebuilding. Even then, it was clear Baalke’s seat was nuclear after the press conference following Tomsula’s sacking took place; 49ers owner Jed York said he told Baalke he was not satisfied with the state of this [the 49ers] team.

Was the team tanking? It wouldn’t be surprising. The 49ers’ lack of spending in free agency both in 2015 and 2016 didn’t make sense then, and it doesn’t make sense now (though there were rumors that players didn’t want to go to the 49ers with all the issues). The same could have been said for the Chip Kelly hire. We’ve already mentioned the offense, but Kelly’s defense under Jim O’Neil was one of the worst in league (not team) history. While the hire was a head-scratcher to begin with, the 49ers didn’t help Kelly get into a position to succeed. Kelly might have been a bad coach no matter what happened, but he was put in a failing situation regardless.

There’s a strange alternate reality of what would have happened if Kelly had stayed with the 49ers for another couple of years and the team only let go of Baalke at the end of the 2016 season. It’s doubtful Kelly’s system would have succeeded no matter what the 49ers would have done, but it’s definitely a weird twilight zone moment.

item.title: 5 Questions with Hogs Haven: The Tea on Colts vs. Commanders in London
item.description: NFL in London, tea and crumpets on the gridiron.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 4 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will travel to London to take on the Washington Commanders. Knowing the party was crossing the Atlantic I sat down with Andrew York (eboracum) of Hogs Haven, SB Nation’s Washington Commanders blog. We swapped questions and answers about both the Commanders and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about this week’s enemy.

You can find my answers to his questions here.

Chris Shepherd: Based on the first three weeks of the season, if you were an offensive coordinator tasked with creating a game plan to attack the Commanders defense, what does your plan look like? What areas of the field are you attacking, what weaknesses are you targeting? How do you beat this Commanders defense?

Andrew York: Well, I’ll start by saying the defense is run by Daronte Jones (not Dan Quinn) and borrows primarily from the Brian Flores defense of the Vikings. It features lots of blitzing, lots of simulated pressures, misdirection, and a complex zone coverage that allows players from any part of the field to either blitz or drop back into coverage. You might normally expect such a defense to be best against the pass, but it is actually strongest at stopping the run, as the last-minute movements and misdirection play havoc with run-blocking keys. As a result, the Commanders are allowing the 3rd-fewest rushing yards (just ahead of the 4th-ranked Vikings) and no rushing TDs so far this season. Where the defense has been weak is against explosive passing plays. I think this is for a few reasons:. 1) the DBs are probably the team’s weakest position group, 2) the complex and shifting zone responsibilities lead to coverage busts by players new to the system, and 3) the scheme just prioritizes sending more people at the QB, which leaves less help on the backend. 

Due to all of this, my gameplan to attack this defense would be to air out the ball as much as possible. Play 3- or even 4-WR sets (forcing Washington’s worst personnel on the field) and layer their routes to hit all areas of the field, expecting a coverage bust somewhere. I’d particularly target Mike Sainristil in coverage, who has had a rough season and has been relegated to primarily slot CB responsibility. The trick here is to protect your QB well enough to enable him to have time to throw. Dallas and Seattle had good enough pass protection that they could air out the ball to the tune of 279 passing yards and 379 passing yards against us respectively. As a primarily zone defense, the Commanders can also struggle against running QBs, as Jalen Hurts demonstrated in week 1. I know Daniel Jones can make plays with his legs, so using some read option might make sense too.

Chris Shepherd: Last week Washington turned in the most surprising upset of the season so far, beating the reigning Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks, 33 to 31. Just looking at the stats of that game, the average person might assume Sam Darnold’s 379 yards passing and four touchdowns would have propelled Seattle over Marcus Mariota’s 183 yard, three touchdown performance but the final score tells a different story. How did the Commanders pull off the upset and do you think those results will be repeatable with Mariota at quarterback?

Andrew York: Well the biggest reason is that Washington didn’t give up any turnovers while securing three turnovers that got converted to TDs (including a pick six). It’s a lot easier to score TDs on a short field set up by your defense and that accounted for 20 of Washington’s 33 points (there was a missed extra point). To add a bit more depth to the answer, despite several key injuries, players were executing at a higher level than in previous weeks, which I mostly attribute to good coaching and players on both sides of the ball being more comfortable in new systems. It is also worth noting that both of Washington’s playcallers (OC David Blough and DC Daronte Jones) are new to playcalling in the NFL and I think they’ve had a bit of a learning curve. Although the team lost Jayden Daniels to injury the previous week, Marcus Mariota is one of the better backup QBs in the NFL and has a similar playstyle to Jayden (mobile QB who can read the field well), so the playbook didn’t have to change much to accommodate him. The turnover differential may have been a bit flukey, but I do have confidence in Mariota to continue to play well and lead the team to victory if the defense can continue to keep games within reach.

Chris Shepherd: Given that Jayden Daniels might miss week four’s game, I was curious about Washington’s ground game without him. In total the Commanders have rushed for a very solid 396 yards (8th most) on 96 attempts, good for 4.1 yards per carry (ranked 16th in the league) in the first three weeks of the season. If you remove Daniels’ 100 yards on 12 carries, the Commanders drop to 296 rushing yards on 84 carries and a rough 3.5 YPC. Last week’s win over the Seahawks saw the Commanders rush 32 times for 82 yards (a 2.6 YPC average). Is this a concern for Washington’s offense moving forward or did the Seahawks just do a good job bottling up an otherwise decent rushing attack?

Andrew York: It’s a bit of a concern and I think there are a few things going on here. First, the OL is decimated by injury right now. LT Laremy Tunsil tore his triceps in Training Camp, forcing the team to move LG Brandon Coleman to LT and weakening both positions. Also, RG Sam Cosmi has been out with a concussion sustained in week 2 (he will not fly to London either). To account for Cosmi’s injury, C Nick Allegretti has moved to RG and Lucas Patrick (signed to the team 2 weeks ago) is starting at Center. So not only has the OL lost its two best players to injury, but 4 players are having to shuffle around to accommodate it. They have still played as a well-coached unit, but that much change has to hurt the run blocking. 

In addition, it’s not like Washington has sunk a lot of resources into the RB room. The two RBs likely to play significant snaps are Jacory Croskey-Merritt (goes by Bill Merritt) and Rachaad White. Bill is an explosive between-the-tackles runner, but weak in pass protection and as a pass catcher and was a 7th-round pick in 2025, so understood to be a bit of a developmental player. White is a much better pass-catching and pass-protecting back, but used a lot less between the tackles and not great at running through contact and a bit of a journeyman RB. So neither are complete backs or difference makers by themselves and can be a bit easy to gameplan against. Worth noting the team just signed RB Austin Ekeler. It’s unlikely he’ll play this week, but he’d add an explosive element while also being a good pass catcher and pass protector if he is ready to suit up.

Chris Shepherd: Can you give me one player on offense and one on defense that Colts fans might not be familiar with who you expect to have an impact on Sunday night?

Andrew York: On offense, I’ll go with RT Josh Conerly Jr. He was the 29th pick of the 2025 NFL draft and although he had a bit of an up-and-down rookie season, he got better as the season went on. He’s continued to build on that momentum and has looked like the best player on the OL right now (with Tunsil and Cosmi sidelined). He didn’t allow a single pressure against a great Seahawks pass rush and looks like the best healthy run blocker on the OL.

On defense, I’ll go with CB Amik Robertson. He’s a 5’9″ stick of dynamite who flies all over the field making plays and had 6 total tackles, 4 passes defended, and a critical forced fumble against the Seahawks last week. He gave up 3 catches for 46 yards and a TD against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but didn’t allow a single catch against any other Seahawks WR. He signed as a free agent from the Lions this offseason and is our most playmaking CB.

Chris Shepherd: How do you predict this game will play out? What does each team do well, where will they struggle and what’s the final score?

Andrew York: When Indy has the ball, I think they will have the most success through the air, as mentioned earlier. Jonathan Taylor vs the Commanders run defense will be a strength on strength matchup, but I mostly expect the Commanders run defense to win that battle and I would expect Taylor to have a relatively quiet game. At the same time, Washington lost LB Leo Chenal to season-ending injury last week and LB Frankie Luvu is likely to be a game-time decision. If Luvu can’t suit up, the run defense might suffer, we’ll see. I expect Indy to do much better passing and picking apart the weak secondary outside of Amik Robertson (and with Safety Nick Cross injured and not traveling to London). In particular, I’d be worried about WR Josh Downs matching up against CB Mike Sainristil in the slot, I wouldn’t be surprised if Downs has a big day.

When Washington has the ball, I think they will try to keep an attack that is pretty balanced in terms of the run and the pass. The strength of the Colts secondary seems to be with boundary CBs Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward, so I wouldn’t be surprised to see Washington scheme up passes to the middle of the field. That actually fits well with the Ben Johnson-style offense that OC David Blough seems to be trying to emulate. I think Washington will have a bit of a tougher time running the ball, but will stay committed to the run and will still find some success on the ground. Overall, I expect Washington to be able to move the ball, but primarily through the air.

Also, it’s worth noting that Commanders fans are very familiar with Daniel Jones from his time on the Giants. For reasons I can’t explain, Daniel Jones seems to have a chip on his shoulder against Washington and always plays his best games against us. He has a 5-3-1 record against Washington that is better than it looks on paper, because he was frequently playing on a Giants team that was collapsing around him. I am not at all taking this game lightly. I always follow the Vegas odds when making score predictions. Vegas currently has the Colts as 3.5-point favorites, so I’d predict a score along the lines of 27-24 in favor of the Colts, with some crazy Daniel Jones plays to keep the Colts in the game and pull off a last-minute win at the end.

And with that, ladies and gentlemen, our week four preview with the enemy is in the books. I want to thank Andrew for giving us the best answers we have received so far this season. Make sure you check out his work over on Hogs Haven, he handles the five questions articles and does a fantastic job with them every week. Hopefully he’s on to something with that final score prediction.

Here’s to an entertaining and injury free game.

As always, go Colts.

item.title: Jerry Jones on Joey Porter Jr. trade: "It's important to think big"
item.description: The Steelers decided to move on from cornerback Joey Porter Jr.
item.content:encoded:
The Steelers decided to move on from cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The Cowboys were ready to pounce.

"It’s important to think big," Cowboys owner and G.M. Jerry Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, "and this is over in that big thought area about what we can do to help our defense."

As to whether other moves will be made this year, Jones said "it's always fluid" and "you can't sit still."

"If you look at the overall picture, I frankly decided a couple of years ago to get in the business of reworking what we are defensively," Jones said.

The Porter trade is about winning now. The question is whether one player will make a big difference. The Cowboys have seen their cornerback play dip since trading linebacker Micah Parsons, and it's not a coincidence. It's easier to cover receivers if the quarterback is rushing to throw — or not throwing at all.

Porter isn't Deion Sanders. (Then again, no one is.) The issue in Pittsburgh was that the two sides had a dramatically different viewpoint as to his value. And the eventual price that Cowboys paid (a sixih-round pick in 2027 and a second-round pick in 2028, with the possibility of a third-round compensatory pick in 2028 if he leave in free agency after this season) reflects the Steelers' assessment of Porter as a player.

Porter's value to the Cowboys remains to be seen. But all signs are pointing to Porter getting his first chance to show what he can do for his new team on Sunday.

item.title: Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers preview: 4 key stats
item.description: A data-driven preview of Lions at Panthers, focusing on key stats and matchups.
item.content:encoded:
This will be the third meeting between the Lions and Panthers in the Dan Campbell era and the first in primetime. Neither of the previous two matchups was decided by fewer than two touchdowns, and Dave Canales, hosting his first primetime game at the helm, will already be the third different Panthers head coach Detroit has faced during that span.

The Panthers may sit at only 1-2, with losses to the Bears and Browns, but they’ve seen some improved play early from to-be-determined franchise quarterback Bryce Young, Jameson Williams’ former quarterback at Alabama, and cannot be taken lightly. After all, Carolina has more recently made the postseason and won its division than Detroit.

The Panthers have finished top five in total free-agent guarantees handed out to defensive players in each of the past two offseasons, committing more than $225 million guaranteed to defensive additions over that span. Yet, despite all that spending and being under the siege of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero, they’re still playing like a bottom-10 unit.

The Lions, already playing their second road primetime game of the season, will look to reverse their fortunes from Buffalo and potentially put together their most complete performance yet during Alim McNeill’s homecoming.

While some rain is expected, much of the analysis consists of passing statistics given the tendencies and personnel of both teams. With that, let’s get into my four key stats and matchups for Sunday night’s game.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus.

Cheaper By the Dozen

The Panthers, in Year 4 of Young, made the switch from head coach Dave Canales to offensive coordinator Brad Idzik as the primary offensive playcaller and have placed more of the load on Young’s shoulders. They’ve had success against the Bears and Falcons defenses but struggled against the Browns. Through three weeks, the Panthers’ 67.9% pass rate ranks third-highest in the league, with Young leading the NFL at 313 passing yards per game. He’ll face a Lions pass defense that ranks dead last with 299.3 passing yards allowed per game, 27th at +0.16 EPA/pass, and 24th with a 48.5% pass success rate allowed.

The Panthers have had even more passing success when they go to 12-personnel, mixing in combinations of Darren Waller, Tommy Tremble, and Mitchell Evans to go along with Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker at wide receiver.

This season, passing from 12-personnel, the Panthers are 20-for-27, a 74.1% completion percentage (8th), for 317 passing yards (2nd) and 11.7 yards per attempt (2nd), with strong analytical metrics as well: a 10.76-yard aDOT (5th), 63.0% success rate (4th), and +0.35 EPA/play (7th). The Panthers’ pressure rate allowed, which overall sits at 52.6% and ranks last in the NFL, drops to only 40.7% (20th) when passing out of 12-personnel. It’s been an added element that Idzik has brought to their offense this season after they didn’t have nearly as much reliance or success with it last year.

The most common targets for Young when passing from 12-personnel have been Tremble (8 targets, 6 catches, 61 receiving yards), Coker (4 targets, 4 catches, 106 receiving yards), McMillan (5 targets, 3 catches, 62 receiving yards), and Waller (3 targets, 3 catches, 43 receiving yards). It’s a potent condensed passing attack for the Detroit Lions to defend.

The Lions defense, which has prided itself on its preference for base defense throughout the majority of the Dan Campbell era—running more of it than anyone last season—has been worked as a pass defense this season, both overall and specifically against 12-personnel.

The Lions pass defense has been getting shredded against 12-personnel:

  • 33 dropbacks (30th, 3rd most)
  • 29 pass attempts (30th)
  • 21 completions (31st)
  • 291 passing yards (32nd)
  • 72.4% completion percentage (26th)
  • 8.8 yards per pass (25th)
  • 4 passing touchdowns (t-31st)
  • 8.41 aDOT (21st)
  • 55.2% passing success rate (19th)
  • +0.38 EPA per play (25th)

Teams have given the Lions a heavy dose of 12-personnel, and they haven’t had answers, all while the Lions’ pressure rate and sack rate are also lower against 12-personnel than they are overall. Kelvin Sheppard will need to equip his defense with better answers against the Panthers. And while the Lions’ cornerback group has been much maligned, having success in coverage against Carolina’s 12-personnel passing attack will also be reliant on improvement from the spine of the defense, with linebackers Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and perhaps Trevor Nowaske or Malcolm Rodriguez, along with safeties Chuck Clark and Christian Izien, needing to execute better.

Young and the Restless

The one area where the Panthers’ passing offense has faltered, as mentioned in the last section, is allowing a league-high pressure rate. Much like Jared Goff and his elite-level processing skills have continued to pick apart the blitz, Bryce Young has found a higher level of success against the blitz so far this season. When defenses don’t bring those additional pass rushers, however, that’s where the Panthers’ prowling passing attack has been declawed.

The Panthers’ yards per pass drop from 8.3 (4th) against the blitz to 6.1 (18th) with no blitz, while their EPA per pass plummets from +0.35 (6th) to -0.09 (21st). Not only does the passing production drop, but the heat applied to Young actually increases. Against the blitz, the Panthers’ pressure rate is 39.5% (t-11th) and their sack rate is only 2.3% (5th). With no blitz, their pressure rate climbs to 45.3% (32nd), while their sack rate jumps to 7.0% (21st). Young and the offense operate more efficiently when he’s sped up and can attack the vacancies left behind in coverage.

The Detroit Lions’ defensive front has shown some teeth early this season, generating a 36.8% pressure rate (3rd) and 6.9% sack rate (12th) when not blitzing. The Panthers were already dealing with backup offensive tackles in Rasheed Walker and rookie Monroe Freeling, and with the injury to left guard Damien Lewis, they’ll be left to play 2024 UDFA Corey Bullock and his 55 career offensive snaps in the first start of his career.

It could be the perfect recipe for disaster for Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, and company to maul the Panthers and leave their passing offense to die in the wilderness—if the coverage behind them can hold up.

It’ll also be on Kelvin Sheppard to calculatedly call off the dogs, rush four, and ask questions later.

Lion Kings of the Jungle

The Carolina Panthers are playing light boxes (six or fewer defenders) on a league-high 40.2% of plays. While defensive tackle Derrick Brown is an imposing player in the middle, the Panthers have been leaving prized free-agent signing Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke—a player exposed by Jahmyr Gibbs against the Giants last season—out to dry in the run defense this season. They’re also relying on undrafted rookie Aaron Hall and fellow rookie Lee Hunter as the two defensive tackles trying to hold down the fort next to Brown on the interior.

Against Man/Duo run concepts, the Panthers have allowed 132 rushing yards on 16 carries and rank league-worst in all of the following: 8.3 yards per carry, four rushing touchdowns, and +0.45 EPA per rush.

Meanwhile, on such runs this season, Gibbs has 12 carries for 61 rushing yards (5.1 yards per carry) and a rushing touchdown, along with an impressive 58.3% rushing success rate. Look for the Lions to go big-on-big, take advantage of the light boxes, and allow Penei Sewell and the re-engineered Detroit People Movers to mash bodies and control the line of scrimmage, giving Gibbs downhill running room all night long.

You’ve Got Air Mail

Even with the weather forecast, the Detroit Lions have a balanced offense, and with the Carolina Panthers without stud cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, they’ll look to take advantage of journeyman Akayleb Evans and rookie Will Lee III filling in.

Teams have only tested the Panthers on 12 deep throws of 20-plus air yards (second fewest) in the NFL, but that should change with the backups in at corner. It’s also worth keeping in mind that in Week 2, the Panthers faced Cooper Rush and rookie UDFA Jack Strand at quarterback. Still, the Panthers are blitzing at a higher-than-expected top-10 rate, and their five deep completions allowed have been costly, resulting in +0.69 EPA per pass (23rd) and 29.8 yards per completion.

Will Lee III has also been beaten deep twice this year, including a 47-yard completion to Rome Odunze on a coverage bust, but also on a badly underthrown ball from Cooper Rush where Lee bit on a double move. I would expect the Lions to strike when the Panthers blitz, particularly if they continue to struggle to generate pressure and leave less support for their unproven corners. When the opportunity is right, Detroit should have a chance to dial up a shot play or two to Jameson Williams. He’s due after all.

item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Chicago Bears
item.description: The Jets are on the road against the Chicago Bears on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The New York Jets face their third NFC North opponent in a row on Sunday, as they are in the Windy City to face the 2-1 Chicago Bears.

New York beat Chicago 31-10 in the last meeting between these teams back in 2022. Prior to that the Jets had last beaten the Bears all the way back in 2000.

Let’s break down the Bears’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

The situation at quarterback is cloudy for the Bears, who may be about to start their third different quarterback in three weeks.

After an inconsistent rookie year, Caleb Williams led the Bears to an 11-6 record last season, and was showing signs of this being his breakout into superstardom when the Bears racked up 59 points in their opener. However, he got injured in week two and the Bears were without him last Sunday, and will be this Sunday as well.

Tyson Bagent had been considered the number two, but he missed practice during the week leading up to last weekend’s game, so the Bears prepared for Case Keenum to lead them against Philadelphia on Monday Night Football. Surprisingly, he put together a terrific performance to lead them to an easy win with 247 yards and two touchdowns.

Ordinarily, you’d expect them to stick with Keenum after a performance like that. However, head coach Ben Johnson has kept his plans under wraps and Chicago beat writers have suggested it may be Bagent who gets the nod this week.

Keenum is obviously more experienced than Bagent, who went 2-2 as a rookie starter in 2023 but has only thrown 15 passes since. Neither offers the same run threat as Williams.

Offensive Line

The Bears had a solid offensive line last season, with no offensive lineman giving up more than three sacks. Three of the five starters are returning, too, as right guard Jonah Jackson, pro bowl left guard Joe Thuney and right tackle Darnell Wright are back after each starting every game last year. They’ve kept the unit strong, as no offensive lineman was credited with giving up any of the six sacks that have been surrendered so far this season.

The center position underwent a change due to Drew Dalman’s sudden retirement but veteran Garrett Bradbury has taken over that role, although he has four penalties in three games.

At left tackle, Braxton Jones remains the number one choice, but he continues to be injury prone after missing considerable time in 2023 and 2025. He’s been ruled out again on Sunday but both Theo Benedet and Ozzy Trapilo started several games in his place last season and they remain on the roster. Benedet filled in for Jones for part of each of the first three games so he figures to start.

The rest of the bench is low on experience as Logan Jones is a rookie second rounder and Luke Newman and Jordan McFadden have started two NFL games between them.

Wright led the Bears with 12 offensive penalties last season.

Running Backs

The Bears currently have the number one running game in the NFL, although Williams being out affects that. D’Andre Swift is seventh in the NFL in rushing yards while Kyle Monangai is averaging 5.9 yards per carry.

They each rushed for 100 yards in the first game, with Monangai doing that in just 10 carries as most of his yardage came on a 61-yard touchdown scamper.

Roschon Johnson remains with the team as a backup although his workload has been reducing over the past few years.

Pass catchers

At wide receiver, the Bears were banking on recent draft picks Rome Odunze and Luther Burden to step up with DJ Moore having been traded after the pair had combined to catch 91 passes last year.

However, early on, it’s been ex-Jets receiver Kalif Raymond who has elevated his game. Johnson was familiar with Raymond from his time in Detroit and brought him over this offseason. So far, Raymond’s role has been bigger than expected as he’s caught 19 passes on 21 targets for a team-high 214 receiving yards.

Burden is also off to a good start as he has 15 receptions already this year. Odunze, on the other hand, only has eight catches, although he is averaging 17.4 yards per catch.

In terms of backups, third round rookie Zavion Thomas and Jahdae Walker each have just one catch for one yard, although Walker’s was for a touchdown.

The Bears have also had good production from their tight ends in recent years with Colston Loveland leading the team with over 700 receiving yards last season and Cole Kmet having posted similar numbers in the past. Both are off to a slow start this year, though.

The third tight end is rookie Sam Roush, who played for Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich at Stanford.

Defensive Line

The Bears have more or less returned most of the edge rotation from last year, but their interior line rotation is completely different other than the returning former pro bowler Grady Jarrett.

The starter alongside Jarrett is Kentavius Street with Neville Gallimore and third round rookie Jordan van den Berg also getting playing time.

The main playmaker on the edge is Montez Sweat, who had 10 sacks last year. The other starter across from him is Dayo Odeyingbo, who already has two sacks after having had just one all year in 2025.

The main reserve on the edge is Austin Booker, who had 4.5 sacks last year, with James Lynch also in the rotation.

Edge Jamree Kromah and defensive tackle Jayden Loving are also on the roster for depth.

Linebackers

2025’s leading tacker Tremaine Edmunds is now with the Giants, so the Bears brought in Devin Bush Jr. to start along with TJ Edwards, who had 67 tackles and five passes defensed in just 10 games last season.

D’Marco Jackson also sees playing time when three linebackers are on the field, but Noah Sewell, who was in the rotation last year, is on the PUP list.

Fifth round rookie Keyshaun Elliott and special teamer Jack Sanborn round out this unit.

Defensive Backs

The Bears’ secondary was the key to their winning record last year as they racked up an incredible 23 interceptions. Even more incredible, though, was their decision to get rid of literally everyone who had more than one.

Pro bowlers Nahshon Wright and Kevin Byard are gone, along with C.J. Gardner-Johnson. To make matters worse, Kyler Gordon is still on the PUP list and safety Coby Bryant is on injured reserve.

It’s perhaps not surprising that they gave up 37 points in their first game of the season with all these changes, but they’ve regrouped well to allow just 16 points in the last two games.

At the safety position, they addressed the need by drafting the athletic Dillon Thieneman in the first round and he’s responded by leading them in tackles through three games.

According to Chicago’s unofficial depth chart, Xavier Woods is listed as the other starting safety. However, Cam Lewis – listed as the starting nickel – has been playing safety instead of him so far this year.

Lewis is listed as doubtful for Sunday, so Woods is likely to make his first start of the year with Elijah Hicks as the third safety and Skyler Thomas available as cover.

At cornerback, Jaylon Johnson is hoping to get back to the level that saw him voted to the pro bowl in 2023 and 2024 before he missed half of last year due to injury. The other starter is Tyrique Stevenson, who broke up 10 passes last year.

Fourth round rookie Malik Muhammad has been the primary slot cornerback so far.

Josh Blackwell and Clark Phillips III are each available for depth.

Special Teams

Literally a quarter of the NFL has a former Jet as their placekicker right now, and the Bears are one of those teams as Cairo Santos has made his home there. Santos’ only miss of the year so far was a blocked chip shot field goal in the Vikings game where there was an issue with the snap count.

Punter Tory Taylor is off to a good start, posting career-best numbers so far with a gross average of over 50 yards per punt.

Raymond was brought in to galvanize the return game and is listed as the number one punt and kickoff returner but, perhaps due to his bigger than expected role on offense, Thomas and Blackwell have been sharing the kickoff return duties.

Walker and Blackwell are the primary punt gunners and Hicks is their most productive tackler so far in kick coverage.

item.title: Broncos vs. 49ers: 3 Players to Watch in Week 4
item.description: In order to defeat the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, these three players need to perform well.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos battle the undefeated San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. Riding the highs of back-to-back comebacks, the Broncos are in pursuit of a third straight win. However, the 49ers present a big challenge for Denver given how good they are on both sides of the ball. In order to achieve a key road victory, these three players will need to perform at a high level.

Bo Nix — Quarterback

Bo Nix boasts a good start to his career. With 26 wins, a dozen game winning drives, and ten fourth quarter comebacks, Nix has certainly outperformed his 2024 NFL Draft peers at the position. He’s arguably the comeback king of the NFL, but fans across Broncos Country are still waiting for more consistency and better starts to games.

I have no doubt a much more consistent rushing attack would benefit the third-year signal caller. However, he simply has to play better. This year, there has been significant regression with Nix’s first and third down passing. Last season, Nix did very well on first downs, but this year’s output is less than optimal. Third-and-short to third-and-medium range passing situations continue to be an issue as well.

Under the guidance of Raheem Morris, the 49ers sport a sound zone-heavy defense that has done a good job of limiting the impact of opposing offenses thus far. They are winning on early downs. They have playmakers that can cover a lot of ground and do well erasing opportunities in down the field and over the middle. I’ll be watching how Nix performs closely on Sunday—he has to have a good start and be a lot more consistent.

Jonah Elliss — Edge Rusher

With Jonathon Cooper sidelined to begin the season on the NFL Commissioner’s Exempt list, the Broncos have been banking on the progression and development of edge rusher Jonah Elliss. The former third-round pick has a significant increase in snaps at nearly 65-percent of the defense’s total—up from 38-percent his first two seasons in Denver.

Unfortunately, through three games Elliss has struggled a fair bit. He doesn’t have a sack and has registered just two hurries and five pressures. We are seeing a significant drop off in hurry and pressure rate. Additionally, containment and setting the edge has been an issue for the former Utah standout. Though I’ll admit that issue hasn’t just been singular to him.

Nobody has been able to sack Brock Purdy thus far. Moreover, the 49ers have one of the best rushing attacks in the league. Will this be the week Elliss steps up and makes some big plays on defense? Denver will need him to play at a high level to keep Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, and Kaelon Black in check.

Alex Singleton — Inside Linebacker

One player I have major concerns about this game is inside linebacker Alex Singleton. I felt Singleton had a rebound performance in Week 2 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. However, I was less than impressed with his outing against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football.

The eighth-year pro has 32 tackles on the season. Though none of them are for loss and he is already credited with 8 missed tackles. Moreover, #49’s numbers in coverage don’t look particular good either. That may be a problem going up against a 49ers team that runs the ball well and is extremely efficient through the air.

49ers Head Coach Kyle Shanahan is a master at finding matchups against opposing defenses that play to his advantage. I have a feeling Shanahan has drawn up a handful of plays that feature players like Christian McCaffrey or George Kittle attempting to expose Singleton’s deficiencies. Alongside the aforementioned Elliss, he is another defender I’ll be keeping close tabs on Sunday.

item.title: Puka Nacua expected back Sunday for Rams, Aaron Donald out
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams get good news and bad news and more NFL news on a Saturday
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams are expected to have Puka Nacua back in the fold, but just as they perhaps get Nacua back, Aaron Donald is out. The Rams will have to find a way to overcome with or without Donald, and they still won’t have Myles Garrett.

It’s another example of this team not playing the way so many envisioned before the start of the season. The idea was a team of star players all playing at together. That hasn’t happened yet.

There’s still time, but in the NFL there’s never enough time. The Rams need to get healthy fast, and they need to win faster if they want to make the postseason.

Talk of the “superteam” is no more.

Rams’ Aaron Donald to miss Week 4 game vs. Eagles, Puka Nacua’s status updated (cbssports)

“Donald unretired this offseason, returning to play for his former team after initially retiring in 2023. The three-time Defensive Player of the Year’s return has not been as smooth as he or the team had hoped. He sat out the opener when the Rams fell to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia, and Sunday will mark his second missed game of the season. Head coach Sean McVay said Donald felt soreness in his back after the team’s Week 3 loss to the Denver Broncos. 

“He’s working as hard as he can to get himself feeling as good as possible. And we’re hopeful and optimistic that good days are ahead,” McVay said. 

When Donald is healthy, he is an offense’s worst nightmare. The 35-year-old’s resume includes a Super Bowl win, eight first-team All-Pro nods and 10 Pro Bowl selections. He has 547 tackles, 111 sacks, 24 forced fumbles and seven fumble recoveries over 11 seasons in his career.“

Rams DT Aaron Donald, TE Terrance Ferguson ruled out vs. Eagles (ramswire)

“The Los Angeles Rams will be missing several key playmakers against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday afternoon. Sean McVay told reporters on Friday that Aaron Donald and Terrance Ferguson have both been ruled out due to injuries. Donald is dealing with a sore back and Ferguson injured his ankle last week against the Denver Broncos.

Additionally, Jaylen Watson has been ruled out, as expected.

Donald’s injury seemingly came out of nowhere. McVay said on Wednesday that he had a sore back and would not practice, but it didn’t appear to be anything serious. It’s unclear when or how the injury occurred. Ferguson went down twice in last week’s loss to the Broncos, injuring his ankle in the first quarter and then again in the second after returning.“

“Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay shares an update on special teams, wide receiver Puka Nacua’s Week 4 practice reps, discusses keys to beating the Philadelphia Eagles, and more.”

item.title: Remembering the Packers’ best performances against the Buccaneers
item.description: Lynn Dickey, Sterling Sharpe, and more headline the best performances against the Buccaneers.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers head to Tampa, Florida this weekend for a date with their old NFC Central opponents, the Buccaneers. 

Setting aside our memories of the 2020 NFC Championship, there were plenty of great matchups between the Packers and Buccaneers over the years, and they produced quite a few high-end statistical performances. Here are some of the best, with links throughout to some highlights that are just about guaranteed to give you a jolt of nostalgia.

Most passing yards – 418 (Lynn Dickey, 1980)

Packers fans should have plenty of good memories of great passing days against the Buccaneers — five different Packers quarterbacks have broken the 300-yard mark against Tampa! But the greatest of them all isn’t Aaron Rodgers or Brett Favre or even Don Majkowski.

It’s Lynn Dickey, who rolled up 418 yards in a game the Packers thoroughly dominated, but didn’t win. Despite outgaining the Buccaneers by more than 300 yards (569 to 262), two turnovers and three missed field goals prevented the Packers from coming out on top. Instead, the game ended in a 14-14 tie, which remains the only tie between these two teams in their relatively long history together.

Most rushing yards – 169 (Ahman Green, 2001)

Ahman Green’s 169 yard day would be more impressive if he could have hung onto the ball. Really, turnovers were the entire theme of the Packers’ 2001 home matchup against their NFC Central opponents — the last time they’d play their division rivals at home before the Buccaneers headed off for the NFC South. 

Green’s fumble was one of three turnovers by the Packers that day and came smack in the middle of a seven-drive series of remarkable futility. After scoring a touchdown on their first drive of the game, the Packers’ next seven drives went like so: punt, interception, punt, fumble, missed field goal, interception, punt.

Yet thanks in part to Green, who scored on a 63-yard scamper in the third quarter, the Packers’ still hung around long enough for one big play to turn the tide later. More on that in a bit. 

Most receiving yards – 169 (Sterling Sharpe, 1989)

In a funny historical coincidence, the Packers’ single-game receiving yardage high against the Buccaneers is the same as their single game rushing yardage high, and somewhat predictably, it belongs to Sterling Sharpe.

Sharpe had 130 or more receiving yards against the Buccaneers four different times, but never put up a bigger yardage number than he did in an eight catch, 169 yard, two touchdown performance against the Buccaneers in 1989.

Sharpe’s performance was the first of three times a Packers player would have 150 or more receiving yards against the Buccaneers, and the other two guys to do it pulled it off in the same game. In 1999, both Bill Schroeder and Antonio Freeman surpassed 150 receiving yards; Schroeder had seven catches for 158 yards, while Freeman had seven catches for just 152, but added two touchdowns, the second a 21-yard strike that gave the Packers the win.

Christian Watson and Matthew Golden: your targets are set for Sunday.

Most points – 24 (Sterling Sharpe, 1993)

Remember earlier when I mentioned Sterling Sharpe had four different games where he put up more than 130 receiving yards against the Buccaneers? Yeah, that 169-yard game was arguably not his best.

In 1993, Sharpe caught 10 passes for 147 yards and scored four touchdowns — three of which came in the first half. The Packers cruised to a 37-14 win behind Sharpe’s massive day.

Most sacks – 4.5 (Bryce Paup, 1991)

Big days aren’t limited to the offense, of course. En route to a 15-13 Packers’ win, Bryce Paup and the rest of the defense put Vinny Testaverde in hell, sacking him seven times, with Paup accounting for 4.5. One of Paup’s sacks came in the end zone, giving him the first (but not only) points of his NFL career. 

Most solo tackles – 10 (two players tied)

Here’s a chance to think about two guys who probably haven’t crossed your mind in a while. The Packers’ high water mark for solo tackles against the Buccaneers is 10 and it’s happened twice. Jude Waddy did it first, taking down 10 players by himself in 1999. Tyrone Williams did it two years later, racking up 10 solo tackles in the same game where Ahman Green ran for 169 yards.

Most interceptions – 2 (eight players tied)

Eight different players have had two interceptions in a game against the Buccaneers, so we’ve got a bunch of different performances from which to choose if we’re looking for a highlight. How’s this one for you?

LeRoy Butler intercepted two passes in the Packers’ 1996 season-opening win over the Buccaneers, setting the tone for their Super Bowl journey.

Oh, and since I have a contractual obligation to mention tight ends whenever possible, Keith Jackson scored three touchdowns that day. Let’s see it again, Tucker Kraft!

Honorable mention: Allen Rossum scores on a punt return to beat the Buccaneers

I mentioned earlier there were some heroics that delivered the win for the Packers in the game where Ahman Green ran for 169 yards, and here they are. After the Packers’ defense forced a punt late in the fourth quarter, Allen Rossum ripped off a 55-yard punt return for a touchdown to give the Packers a 21-20 win over the Buccaneers in 2001. Was it a pretty game? Certainly not. But Rossum’s effort gave the Packers an exciting win over Tampa in their last meetings as divisional rivals, and that’s always going to be worth remembering.

Patrick Mahomes, Chiefs have rediscovered the deep pass | ESPN

Mahomes struggled much of last season to connect with his pass catchers on deep passes. He completed only 42 of his 101 attempts in which the ball traveled at least 15 yards. His 41.6% completion percentage ranked 19th in the league. Mahomes also threw more interceptions (five) than he had touchdowns (two) on such throws.

The Chiefs’ deep-passing attack should be tested in Sunday’s game against the Raiders, who have created a league-high nine takeaways, including four interceptions.

Jerry Jeudy has disappeared from Browns offense: Five teams that could trade for WR | CBS Sports

Kansas City Chiefs

While the Chiefs did not invest in any wide receiver help in the offseason, they have the look of an offense that could benefit from another weapon out wide or in the slot. Jeudy and Rashee Rice can both move around in the formation while Xavier Worthy remains a deep threat and YAC accumulator out wide. The depth in this group is minimal, and the top two have been just as active as pass-catchers as running back Kenneth Walker III and tight end Travis Kelce, so the wait for one of them to emerge as a go-to target continues (and may never end). With this team squarely back in the Super Bowl conversation, it needs to both maximize its wide receiver output and add insurance behind the starters in order to prevent late-season regression.

Kansas City Chiefs DC Steve Spagnuolo dropped a grenade ahead of Week 4 vs. the Las Vegas Raiders, and fans have reason to worry | A to Z Sports

“Well, we were on a course to kind of keep Chamarri (Conner) in one spot,” Spagnuolo said. “I don’t know if we’re still there now or not. Listen, both Jaden (Hicks) and Alohi (Gilman) have done an admirable job. They would have liked to have some plays back in the Miami game. Obviously, on those deep throws, and the one that we could have caught. But Chamarri, listen, I think I’ve said this before, but it seems like every year he’s been here and we’ve done cut-ups at the end of the season, and we’re looking through the film, 27 keeps showing up, making plays. So, hopefully we can get him back there doing that.”

And when you have a guy like Andy Reid calling the plays and putting them in good positions, it offers a lot of challenges.

Three Different Ways Chiefs Can Work to Ensure a Win vs. Raiders on Sunday | Sports Illustrated

According to TruMedia, Vegas is seventh in total turnover EPA with 10.73.

The Chiefs have done a very respectable job protecting the rock thus far. Their plus-three turnover differential is tied for the fourth-best figure in the sport, and they’re in the upper half of the league with just a pair of giveaways (both interceptions by quarterback Patrick Mahomes). In hostile territory, not coughing up the rock would force Las Vegas’ offense to capitalize on a higher clip of its possessions.
