item.title: 5 Good Questions with Big Blue View: What are the Giants fans thoughts on the Harbaugh era?
item.description: Breaking down the New York Giants with Big Blue View.
item.content:encoded:
Happy Saturday one and all.

Ed Valentine, the longtime leader of Big Blue View was kind enough to bring out of retirement the “Five Questions with the Enemies” so lets get to know the New York Giants a little better.

Enjoy.

Q: Are you satisfied with the team’s moves after the Jaxson Dart injury?

Well, I think the Giants were aggressive in trying to make the quarterback room the best it can be without the No. 1 guy. They used a fifth-round pick to acquire J.J. McCarthy. Now, there are a lot of opinions about McCarthy, and nobody knows if he will become Sam Darnold, Trey Lance, or something in-between. I think Giants fans should be heartened by the fact that the team was aggressive in addressing a problem.

For the Giants, it still comes down to whether or not Jameis Winston can handle the job. They gave Winston a two-year, $13 million extension right before the season started. I have a hard time believing they will hurry to replace him, although there is already a lot of “when will McCarthy start?” chatter.

Who is going to be counted on most to help negate the loss of Brian Burns?

Well, former No. 3 overall pick Abdul Carter is going to have to assert himself. Kayvon Thibodeaux will play more. Maybe Arvell Reese will be used more as a rusher. It is going to be incumbent upon defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, though to be more creative than he has been over the first three weeks to put rushers in better situations.

Arvell Reese was a hotly debated prospect among Cardinals fans, what has he shown the first month of the season and how do you feel about his long term outlook?

Reese is going to be a star. He isn’t there yet, but he will get there. This guy is absurdly physical. He can run. He can tackle in space. He can cover. He has pass rush potential. He wants to work at it and get better. It won’t be long before he is a dominant player. 

What is the overall feeling as the John Harbaugh era has gotten underway?

Optimism. Harbaugh has brought professionalism, expectations, the ability and willingness to make players understand the hard work required. The Giants aren’t a “clown show” anymore.

The Cardinals are slight road favorites, Is that more a concern about the Giants offense or defense in your opinion?

I don’t know. It is a bit of a surprise to me. Still, the Giants have lost their quarterback and their best defensive player the past two weeks. It’s probably a bit of both. The Giants are coming off a game in which they scored only 12 points, so I get the concern on that side.

item.title: Chicago Bears Week 4 Flashbacks: Bengals Blowout, Hester sets a record, and more!
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 4 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
It’s week 4, a week that has seen many a classic Bears games! Luckily we have some hallmark games from the past to uncover today. Climb aboard Gridiron Time Machine for a trip down memory lane!

1.) 1986, Bears @ Bengals: Chicago overwhelms Cincinnati in a 44-7 rout

Coming off one of the most dominant seasons in NFL history, the 1986 Bears entered Week 4 looking every bit like a team capable of doing it all over again.

The unfortunate team standing in their way was the Cincinnati Bengals.

Chicago jumped out to a 21-0 first-quarter lead behind a banged up Jim McMahon rushing touchdown and touchdown passes to Walter Payton and Willie Gault. McMahon would add another touchdown pass to Emery Moorehead in the second half, finishing with 211 yards and three scores through the air.

Gault was the star through the air, hauling in 174 receiving yards, while the Bears piled up 476 yards of total offense and 222 yards on the ground.

The defense was not exactly taking the afternoon off either.

Chicago intercepted Boomer Esiason four times and forced five turnovers overall, holding Cincinnati to seven points in a 44-7 blowout.

The win moved the defending champions to 4-0, continuing a start in which it looked like the rest of the NFL might once again be playing for second place.

That eventually changed, but on this afternoon the Bears looked every bit as terrifying as the team that had just steamrolled its way through 1985.

2.) 2011, Bears vs. Panthers: Forte runs wild and Hester makes history

The Bears entered Week 4 at 1-2 and badly needed a win after dropping back-to-back games to the Saints and Packers.

Matt Forte and Devin Hester made sure they got one.

Forte gashed Carolina from the start, including a 46-yard run on Chicago’s opening possession and a 17-yard touchdown in the second quarter. He would finish with a career-high 205 rushing yards while adding another 23 through the air, accounting for 228 of Chicago’s 317 total yards.

Then there was Hester.

With Chicago leading 17-10, Hester fielded a punt and raced 69 yards for a touchdown, giving the Bears a 24-10 advantage. It was the 11th punt return touchdown of his career, setting a new NFL record.

The defense chipped in as well, with D.J. Moore returning a Cam Newton interception 20 yards for a touchdown in the first quarter (no not THAT D.J. Moore, but it is pretty interesting that Cam Newton has thrown touchdown passes to multiple people named “D.J. Moore). Carolina still piled up a franchise-record 543 yards of offense, but the Bears found enough big plays on defense and special teams to stay in front.

Forte helped put the game away with a 40-yard run late in the fourth quarter, and Chicago escaped Soldier Field with a 34-29 victory.

It was about as Bears of a victory as you could draw up.

Run the football, steal a score on defense, then let Devin Hester do Devin Hester things.

3.) 2018, Bears vs. Buccaneers: Trubisky trounces the Bucs for 6 touchdowns

There might not be another game that better sums up the highs of the Mitchell Trubisky era.

Through the first three games of the 2018 season, Trubisky had thrown just two touchdowns, and questions were already starting to build about whether Matt Nagy’s new offense was actually going to unlock the second-year quarterback.

Then Tampa Bay came to Soldier Field.

Trubisky absolutely torched the Buccaneers.

He threw five touchdown passes in the first half alone, becoming the first quarterback in Bears history to accomplish that feat. By the time his afternoon was over, Trubisky had completed 19-of-26 passes for 354 yards, six touchdowns and a 154.6 passer rating.

Those six touchdowns went to five different receivers, with Tarik Cohen adding 121 receiving yards as the Bears built an absurd 38-3 halftime lead.

The defense joined in on the fun against a Tampa Bay offense that entered the week leading the NFL in both total and passing yards. Khalil Mack recorded his fourth straight game with a strip-sack, while Chicago forced three turnovers and sacked Buccaneers quarterbacks four times.

Chicago cruised to a 48-10 win, with Trubisky’s six touchdown passes finishing just one shy of Sid Luckman’s franchise record of seven set in 1943.

The win moved the Bears to 3-1 heading into their bye week and gave us the first real glimpse of what Nagy’s offense could look like when everything clicked.

Unfortunately, six-touchdown games never became the norm.

But for one afternoon at Soldier Field, Mitchell Trubisky looked completely unstoppable.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: J.J. McCarthy, cornerback help, Arvell Reese, more
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions, answers about the Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Lawrence Kenney asks: With the trade for McCarthy, we assume his rookie contract, but does it include his option year? Assuming we can help rehabilitate his career, this could be an attractive trade chip. 

Ed says: Yes, the Giants also get the fifth-year option. It is part of the standard rookie contract for first-round picks.

Jim Eggers asks: Please explain to me how Nubin can look so absolutely clueless playing safety in the NFL.  He had a great college career at Minnesota.  Senior year 1st team All American with 13 career interceptions and was a tackling machine. A plug and play guy for sure, right. Not exactly. In the NFL he has no coverage skills, he is very slow, no situational awareness,  just overmatched. No coaching will help this guy.

Ed says: Jim, I think you are being a bit harsh. Tyler Nubin has clearly not been the player the Giants hoped he would be when they drafted him. He has been below average, and has not been the ball-hawking playmaker the Giants thought they were getting. You make it seem as though he doesn’t belong in the league. I’m not willing to go there.

Rob Stolzer asks: With Burns now out for the year, will we be seeing Reese shifted over to the edge position for more plays?

Ed says: Rob, it is an option. Pro Football Focus says Reese has aligned outside on 30 of 177 snaps (16.9%). Maybe that ticks up some based on situations. There have been times when Reese and Abdul Carter have switches, simply to get Carter pass rushing over a guard. Reese, though, will remain primarily an inside linebacker.

Honestly, the pass rush remains an underdeveloped area of Reese’s game. Per PFF, he has rushed just 17 times so far. His 5.9% pressure rate is 137th out of 200 grades off-ball linebackers or edge defenders. That is a small sample size, but perhaps an indication that Reese is a work in progress as a pass rusher.

I think the Giants signed Jihad Ward to be their third edge defender.

Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, I probably missed it but I don’t remember much hype about Holland in the off season other than the Leadership Council and the contract extension. There were other players (e.g. Carter, Reese, and Sisi) I remember people talking about but not so much Holland. He’s emerging as a leader on and off the field. What did I miss?

Ed says: Kölner, you didn’t miss anything. Holland didn’t make a lot of plays for the Giants a year ago, and since his career-high in interceptions for a season was two entering this year there was doubt he would become a big-time playmaker. Well, he has.

Chase Baldwin asks: We traded for J.J. McCarthy in the wake of this I saw BBV split between this is horrendous, and he’ll be taking over starting soon. A few people sat in the middle and think he’s a fine #2. My question is word got out Monday afternoon, J.J. has to get from Minnesota to NY what does that look like ? Does he just hop on a plane with a few belongings and ship his stuff to NY? Do teams trading a player usually give them a heads up it could happen and to maybe pack up their things ? Just curious about the logistics of him actually getting settled in NY. 

Ed says: Chase, per the Collective Bargaining Agreement, teams are required to pay travel and moving expenses when they acquire a player. Teams also generally provide players with short-term living arrangements until they are able to find their own places. Teams often help arrange travel plans for new players.

Players find out about trades when they get traded. Teams don’t give players a heads up that they might get traded, although players can often figure that out on their own.

Chris Milner asks: What’s your sense of the progress that the Giants are making in building a playoff and championship contender? Are they moving the needle, or are they just struggling to get by with all the injuries?

Ed says: Chris, the answer is actually in your question. They are “building” a championship contender. They are not, and never were going to be, a championship contender this year. The injuries put them in survivial mode for this season. But, the culture that has been established, the quality young players they have added, and what John Harbaugh learns about what this team needs going forward are all part of the process.

Jason Zalewski asks: Why do you think we’ve been so poor at drafting early round CBs? Feels like we’ve been in CB purgatory since our SB wins. The jury is still out on Tae Banks.

Ed says: Jason, have the Giants been bad at drafting early-round cornerbacks? It is way too early to judge Colton Hood. Dru Phillips, a third-round pick, is a good player. Cor’Dale Flott played well last year. It really isn’t fair to go back beyond Joe Schoen’s tenure as GM.

Schoen has one miss in Banks, and even that might still be salvaged.

Fletcher Wyman asks: Cutting through all the JJ noise and looking at a specific position of need I’ll ask you directly what you think of the possibility of trading for Riley Moss, mimicking a feed post I made today. He’s a 26yo starter that will be a UFA in 2027. He is very good against the run and plays opposite of Surtain so he’s targeted at a very high rate. He’s considered grabby but is middle of the pack for penalties vs targets. Denver may be interested in gaining assets before he has the opportunity to test the market.

Ed says: Fletcher, I won’t claim to have studied Moss. The Broncos are a Super Bowl contender, though. Why would they trade a starting player off their defense when they are in win-now mode? I am in favor of adding good players. What’s the cost, financially and in draft capital? You don’t trade for him without giving him a long-term contract? Does acquiring him get in the way of letting Colton Hood develop?

I’m not sure I see this one as realistic.

Roy Koeslag asks: I know with all of the injuries to key players at the Giants, the thoughts on how we can solve the season must be ongoing. Trading for QB McCarthy seems like a risk because we don’t have a lot of picks next year. Signing a veteran QB with a similar profile as Dart would have been a better option in my opinion. Do you think they will try to add a veteran CB to help out? That seems like a much more urgent hole in our team.

Ed says: Roy, the Giants traded for McCarthy because they believed he has more upside than anyone they could have signed as a free agent or taken off a practice squad. I appreciate the aggression. Will it pay off? Nobody knows.

As for cornerback, I think it’s a wait-and-see deal. Can Greg Newsome keep playing well? What will Tae Banks provide when he is is healthy again? How will Colton Hood develop? Will Paulson Adebo help when he returns?

I think the Giants need to be very careful about giving away draft assets. The focus still has to be on the future. Giving away assets that compromise the future for short-term fixes that — maybe — help you win one or two more games this year doesn’t seem like a good plan.

Stephen Goodyear asks: Understand and agree with the aversion to a Porter acquisition. But it seems we have CB issues. First, injury updates on Adebo and Banks please? Secondly, Newsome seems OK. Holland seem positioned improve by playing. Then what? If either Holland or Newsome gets injured. Jones? Washington?

Ed says: Another cornerback question. Stephen, I think Banks might play this weekend. Adebo is on IR. He can’t return until at least Week 6. I don’t know if he will. Jevon Holland is a safety, so he shouldn’t be part of the conversation.

In the short term, I think the Giants just have to ride with Colton Hood and let him develop. He is being forced to play more than anticipated due to injuries. In the long run, that might help him.

Could the Giants trade for a cornerback? If they do, I would think they would be looking for a player who would be a multi-year acquisition. They might just have to get by the best they can, and then try to address it in the offseason.

Brian Scott asks: In past years we’ve seen various members of the front office — Joe Schoen and Brandon Brown, for example — at college games, ostensibly scouting players of interest. I don’t recall hearing as much about this lately. Is this still a thing?

Ed says: Brian, of course it is a thing. That is their job. I just don’t spend a lot of time chasing the “where is Joe Schoen this weekend?” stuff. He is going to be in as many places as he can be, as often as he can be. Giants scouts will be, and have been, at games across the country every weekend.

Roger VanWart asks: Ed, the Giants have 5 games and a by week before the trade deadline. How much will the W/L record effect if the Giants on if they are  buyers or sellers at the deadline? Or will play on the field be the determining factor. It’s hard to judge a team when the top 2 offensive and defensive players were in less than 3 games.

Ed says: Roger, isn’t the won-loss record reflective of the quality of play on the field? Of course if the Giants get to midseason and they sense a chance to sneak into the playoffs they will be tempted to be more aggressive at the trade deadline.

I will keep reiterating, though, that they have to remember that unless Jameis Winston or J.J. McCarthy suddenly m0rphs into an All-Pro quarterback there is a ceiling on this year. They have to keep the future in mind and not waste assets for short-term fixes that could be used to help build for next season and beyond.

Gregory Riley asks: Who is your favorite Giants announcer of all time?

Number 1 for me is Marty Glickman (showing my age) as he had such a commanding voice and made you think you were actually at the game. Second would be Jim Gordon “Wide right Giants win Giants win.” 

Ed says: Greg, I probably can’t answer that question. I like the current guys, Bob Papa and Carl Banks. I remember listening to Dick Lynch.

Let me throw that one out to the community. Let us know who you really liked listening to.

Rafael Gonzalez asks: I’ve got a question about something the Giants talked about all offseason: getting those defensive linemen’s hands up and batting down passes when they can’t get to the quarterback. Well, we’re several games into the season, the D-line isn’t exactly getting home consistently, and I’m STILL waiting for their FIRST defensive-line pass deflection!

So what happened to that whole “get your hands up” emphasis? If you’re not getting enough pressure, shouldn’t batting down passes be one of the easiest ways to impact the passing game? Are the coaches still emphasizing it, and if they are, why aren’t we seeing it? Because right now, it sure looks like another area where the Giants talked about something all offseason but aren’t getting the results on Sunday. I’d really like to hear what you guys think about this.

Ed says: Rafael, this is really something defensive linemen are taught from the time they start playing the position. It’s not like the Giants emphasize it more or less than any other team in the league.

The fact that they have just one batted pass (by Tremaine Edmunds) doesn’t mean they aren’t getting their hands up. You can get your hands up and not have the quarterback hit them with the ball. All of the same things apply to talking about why the Giants haven’t gotten enough sacks. The Giants are last in the league in quarterback pressure rate (10.5%). When they put more pressure on the quarterback, they will get better results.

Richard Norato asks: Hi Ed, in your opinion which NFL coaches past or present did the best job of keeping their teams on task when adversity or disaster struck.

Ed says: Richard, I think you just go down the list of the best coaches of all-time, the guys who did it successfully for a long time, and you realize that is something they all had to be good at.

Mike Tomlin had to be great at that to never have a losing season. Tom Coughlin was great at it. The ability handle adversity is one of the things that make great coaches great.

Ken Silver asks: How badly did losing the speedy jitterbug Austin hurt us since we have no other player like that and no explosive player on offense besides Nabers who is still working his way back from major knee surgery, and can we make better/more use of Mooney? Never going deep and threatening a defense with having to cover more of the field let’s them off the hook, can we throw the ball downfield sometimes since it might create more opportunity for short stuff and improve the running game, and b/c it seems like there’s a 50/50 chance of defensive pass interference?

Ed says: Ken, there is no doubt that losing Austin hurt. The Giants have no other player with the yards after catch skillset and quickness of Austin.

Let’s see how the passing game develops. There is no doubt the Giants need more explosive plays. They can’t go the hard way every time.

Glen Boshart asks: Even though I doubt no one has asked this yet, what the heck happened to James? I mean, the coaches had plenty to look at during the preseason, if his arm is shot they most certainly should have seen that. Same if he doesn’t fit the scheme. Yet they extended him. Is he hurt? And if he is, I’d love to see what the other QB not named McCarthy get a shot. He looked good in preseason, which is why they signed him.

Ed says: Glen, the mystery with Winston has been some of the throws that have been low or well short. I wonder if he is so conscious of not turning the ball over, especially in the elements last Sunday, that he has been guiding the ball a bit. Let it play out.

The extension tells us they believe in him, at least to a point. Nobody plans on having their backup quarterback play 16 games.

item.title: The Browns are making their presence felt in the AFC North
item.description: An exciting start to the Cleveland Browns season put them at the top of the AFC North
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns are currently sitting atop the AFC North with a 3-1 record. It is an unexpected start for many Browns fans, especially after the struggles against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week One. It was a very dramatic Thursday Night Football game in which Cleveland drove the ball down the field in the final minutes to put itself in a good position to kick a field goal for the win. This win makes it the first time the Browns have led in the AFC North since 2021.

The Cleveland defense has continued to prove they are a strong unit. This group recorded two interceptions and five sacks in the matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers. They made crucial stops and continued to pressure the opposing offense.

item.title: Rams don't have a timeline on Myles Garrett's return
item.description: Despite a report that Rams defensive end Myles Garrett would miss about six weeks with his knee injury, head coach Sean McVay says the team isn't working on a timeline that specific.
item.content:encoded:
Despite a report that Rams defensive end Myles Garrett would miss about six weeks with his knee injury, head coach Sean McVay says the team isn't working on a timeline that specific.

Asked how Garrett is doing after knee surgery, McVay said Garrett is doing well but told reporters the team does not have any time frame for when he will actually be back on the field.

"Myles is good. I've seen him in there, he physically looks good," McVay said. "He's got a good look in his eye. It's been good having him in and out of a lot of the meetings while he's attacking his rehab. He's making good progress, but as far as a specific timeline, I'm not ready to give you guys that. As soon as I have those things I'll give you guys updates."

After sitting out practice with a knee injury in training camp and struggling to play on his injured knee in the Rams’ Week 1 loss to the 49ers, Garrett had surgery and was placed on injured reserve. By rule, players on injured reserve have to miss at least four weeks, but it appears that Garrett will be out longer than that. How much longer, the Rams still don't know.

item.title: Is front-office pride endangering yet another Bengals season?
item.description: Cincinnati desperately needs help at a position the team refuses to address.
item.content:encoded:
Pride comes before the fall. And if the Cincinnati Bengals keep refusing to make the changes they desperately need, that is exactly what is going to happen.

The Bengals need a linebacker who can cover tight ends and running backs. Their pride is keeping them from getting one.

Sunday’s 30-27 loss to Pittsburgh put that weakness on display again. Aaron Rodgers’ first pass went to running back Jaylen Warren on a short crossing route and became a 30-yard gain. Where was the linebacker?

By the end of the afternoon, Warren had three catches for 49 yards. Tight ends Darnell Washington, Pat Freiermuth and Robert Tonyan combined for six receptions and another 99 yards. That is nine catches for 148 yards from running backs and tight ends, which was more than half of Rodgers’ passing yardage.

The Bengals cannot keep watching opponents exploit the same weakness and insist the answer is already in the building.

Washington delivered the most expensive reminder. With the game tied in the fourth quarter, he turned a reception into a 47-yard gain on the possession that produced Pittsburgh’s winning field goal. Cincinnati needed to get someone on the ground. Instead, a tight end helped move the Steelers into scoring position.

Some of that was tackling. Some of it was defending receivers in space. Both require attention, and neither gets corrected by pretending the current personnel simply need more time.

A week earlier, Dalton Schultz caught 12 passes for 140 yards against the Bengals. Cincinnati won in Houston, but the result concealed a problem that Pittsburgh brought back into focus. A win does not turn a defensive weakness into a strength.

The Bengals have enough evidence. What they need now is the willingness to admit their linebacker room needs help.

That admission should not be difficult. Teams make personnel decisions, evaluate the results, and adjust. Bringing in a veteran does not require abandoning young players. It requires acknowledging that development and winning this season have to happen together.

Instead, Cincinnati is letting pride protect its decisions while opposing offenses collect the benefits.

There are options worth pursuing, starting with Shaq Thompson. Buffalo currently lists him on its practice squad, and PFF’s player page gives him a 69.2 coverage grade for 2025, 14th among 88 qualified linebackers. That is enough of a reason to make a call.

Jerome Baker deserves consideration as well. He remains on the latest available free-agent list, and his 69.1 coverage grade last season makes him worth examining, even with the limitation of a smaller workload. Bring him in and find out whether he can help.

These players are candidates, and the Bengals have work to do before deciding whether either belongs on their roster. They need to assess health, movement, and the ability to handle the assignments that are causing trouble: carrying a tight end through a route and staying with a running back coming out of the backfield.

That work should already be underway.

The standard cannot be whether a signing validates the Bengals’ offseason plan. The standard has to be whether it improves their defense.

Cincinnati does not need to hand a veteran a starting job or promise him every snap. It needs to create competition for the passing-down assignments its current players are failing to handle consistently. If an available linebacker can do that job better, he should be on the field.

Joe Burrow’s prime is too valuable to spend protecting the front office’s pride. The Bengals have a weakness, their opponents know it, and help is worth investigating.

Admit the need. Make the calls. Give this team a better chance to win.

item.title: A look back at the Colts’ international game history
item.description: The Colts return to London in Week 4 after previous regular-season trips to London, Frankfurt and Berlin.
item.content:encoded:
The Colts are heading overseas again.

Indianapolis will face the Washington Commanders in London in Week 4, marking the franchise’s fourth regular-season international game and its third trip overseas in the last four seasons. What once felt like a rare event has quietly become a fairly regular part of the Colts’ schedule.

The franchise has played internationally before in the preseason, including a 2005 American Bowl matchup against the Falcons in Tokyo, but the more interesting history begins with the regular-season games. The Colts have already played in London, Frankfurt and Berlin, and they enter this weekend with a 2-1 record outside the United States.

Here is a look back at how those regular season games played out before Indianapolis returns to London.

2016: Jaguars 30, Colts 27 — London

The Colts’ first regular-season international game came in 2016 against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium.

Indianapolis fell behind 23-6 before making a late push, scoring three touchdowns in the fourth quarter and getting within three points. Andrew Luck threw for 234 yards and two touchdowns, but the comeback fell short as Jacksonville held on for a 30-27 win.

It was also an AFC South game, which made the stakes a little different from the usual international matchup. The Colts were technically the road team and left London at 1-3 after a frustrating start to the season.

The NFL’s international operation was still much smaller at the time. London games were becoming more common, but Germany had yet to enter the rotation and the league had not expanded its overseas schedule anywhere close to what it looks like today.

For the Colts, it was their first taste of regular-season football abroad, and it ended with a loss.

2023: Colts 10, Patriots 6 — Frankfurt

Seven years later, the Colts finally returned overseas, this time to Germany.

The result was much better, even if the football itself was not particularly memorable.

Indianapolis beat New England 10-6 in Frankfurt in one of the stranger games of the 2023 season. Gardner Minshew threw for only 194 yards, the Colts scored one touchdown and the two teams combined for just 16 points.

Jonathan Taylor scored Indianapolis’ only touchdown, while the defense did most of the work. The Colts intercepted Mac Jones late in the fourth quarter before New England eventually turned to Bailey Zappe for its final possession.

It was not pretty, but nobody asks how an international win looks afterward.

The victory gave the Colts their first regular-season win outside the United States and evened their international record at 1-1.

2025: Colts 31, Falcons 25 (OT) — Berlin

The Colts did not have to wait another seven years for their next trip.

Indianapolis faced Atlanta in Berlin last season, playing in the first NFL regular-season game ever held in the German capital. Unlike the previous two international games, the Colts were the designated home team.

This one was easily the most entertaining of the three.

The game went to overtime tied at 25 before Indianapolis finished it with a touchdown to earn a 31-25 victory. The win improved the Colts to 2-1 internationally and gave them consecutive victories in Germany after the 2023 win in Frankfurt.

It was also part of what has become a much larger NFL push into Europe. Germany has quickly become one of the league’s biggest international markets, and the Colts have now been involved in games in two different German cities.

For a franchise that went seven years between its first and second regular-season international appearances, the trips have suddenly started piling up.

2026: Back to London

If the previous three trips are any indication, expecting another close game would make sense. Every Colts regular-season international game has been decided by six points or fewer. They lost 30-27 to Jacksonville in 2016, beat New England 10-6 in Frankfurt and needed overtime to beat Atlanta 31-25 in Berlin last season.

The settings have changed, the opponents have changed and the quality of football has certainly varied, but the Colts have never had an easy afternoon overseas. Even the 2023 Patriots game, which was not exactly an offensive showcase, stayed undecided until the final minutes.

There is also an element of unpredictability that comes with these games. The travel schedule is different, the routine during the week changes and both teams are playing in an environment they do not normally experience during the season. That does not automatically make every international game close, but the Colts’ history suggests they have rarely been comfortable either way.

Indianapolis comes into this one trying to build off its win over Houston after an 0-2 start, so another one-score game would hardly be surprising. The Colts have already played two tight games in the last two weeks, and their international history has followed the same pattern.

Ten years after their first London trip, the Colts are back in England with a 2-1 regular-season international record and a chance to make it three straight wins overseas. Based on how their previous trips have gone, they may have to sweat through another one to get there.

item.title: Panthers vs Lions: 5 Questions with Pride of Detroit
item.description: Get the Detroit-style view of Week 4's game
item.content:encoded:
Week 4 of the young 2026 NFL season already has the Carolina Panthers and Detroit Lions trending in different directions. The Lions are playoff contenders and quiet Super Bowl hopefuls. Your 2025 NFC South champions, on the other hand, are just hoping that there are fewer injuries in the 13 weeks after their Week 5 bye than there were in the four weeks prior to it.

That doesn’t mean that Lions fans are taking this week for granted or that the Lions themselves haven’t struggled with their more fair share of inuries. Ryan Matthews from Pride of Detroit answered five of my questions about the Lions to try to give us their side of this story. These answers were the sober, attentive reflections of a fan whose team has only very recently known success, at least relative to their history. In short, they did not fill me with confidence and optimism in the Panthers chances of catching Detroit in the midst of a cat nap.

The Carolina Panthers are quite literally half the team they expected to be when they started training camp. How are the Lions faring with the injury bug this deep into the 2026 season?

The Lions’ 2026 roster has bites going back to 2025 that have really put them in a bind on the backend of their defense. Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, once considered to be the top safety duo in the NFL, suffered season-ending injuries last season, and they’re still on the PUP heading into this Week 4 matchup. Detroit’s secondary has been lit up three straight weeks in a row, and while the cornerbacks haven’t been playing their best ball, missing both Joseph and Branch in their respective safety positions has made for some tough viewing when the Lions defense takes the field.

Avonte Maddox, a veteran defensive back, was re-signed to compete for a spot in Detroit’s secondary. He earned it in the summer. Maddox played some free safety, box safety, and in the slot as a nickelback to start the season, but he suffered an injury in Week 2 that put him on injured reserve for the foreseeable future. Thomas Harper is another player who played his way into a spot in the secondary, but he, too, suffered an ankle injury in Week 2’s game against Buffalo that put him on IR as well. That leaves Chuck Clark, a veteran on his fourth stop in as many seasons, to hold down the single-high safety looks for the most part, and safeties coach Jim O’Neil trusts him in that role. Alongside him is Christian Izien, a player who looked like he was shot out of a cannon in his season debut last week against the Jets. Izien had a groin injury crop up at the end of training camp, but he’s a guy who many expected to play the Branch role: box safety, in the slot, up near the line of scrimmage. Izien led the Lions in tackles (11) and finished second in defensive stops (4) against the Jets in Week 3.

Unfortunately—or fortunately depending on how you’re looking at it—Panthers fans won’t get to see the return of Cade Mays this weekend in Carolina after he had a freak wrist injury near the beginning of camp. Otherwise, the Lions have been pretty fortunate with injuries!

The Lions are already on their second offensive coordinator since Ben Johnson left for the Chicago Bears. What are your hopes and worries three games into the Drew Petzing era?

For all the “Dan Campbell is a Ben Johnson merchant” and “Detroit sure misses Ben Johnson” talk, Drew Petzing’s offense has hung 31 points in three consecutive weeks. After a bit of a slow start in terms of opening drives and third-down efficiency, the early returns on Petzing are pretty promising. Jared Goff looks comfortable in the offense, getting into favorable checks and commanding the group. The offensive line dealt with some injuries in the first couple of weeks to their starting left guard—Christian Mahogany—and starting right tackle—rookie Blake Miller—but they looked like a really solid and steady unit when they returned in Week 3.

Some mild concerns for me, and they’re admittedly a bit nitpicky, are play calls near the goal line. Last week, nearing the end of the half and the Jets with just one timeout remaining, Detroit called a designed rollout for Goff on first down that he effectively threw away and a fade route to Amon-Ra St. Brown that did result in a touchdown. It left the Jets with 1:36 on the clock and a timeout still at their disposal, but would’ve liked to see the Lions get to their bread and butter by running the football, forcing the Jets to burn their timeout, and playing with their aggressive, four-down approach on offense. Which seems to run counterintuitive to my second nitpick about the offense: the number of run plays on second-and-10. Petzing’s explanation referred back to Detroit’s four-down approach on offense, but against the Bills, it felt like Buffalo knew it was coming, but Detroit still stuck with it, leaving them in plenty of third-and-long situations.

Again, early results are trending in a positive way, those concerns are mild at most, but the Lions feel like they’re in a much better spot on offense than they were a season ago.

What’s with barely beating the Saints and the Jets? I thought y’all were supposed to be a good team.

Is the suggestion here that the Saints and Jets aren’t good football teams? Because New Orleans went into Baltimore and took home a victory, and then they nearly pulled out last week’s game against a 3-0 Las Vegas Raiders team. The Jets are some clock mismanagement away from being a 2-1 football team themselves, so I think Detroit has actually played some pretty tough teams that will challenge for the playoffs in their respective conferences.

A rain game where one team is looking to establish a struggling rushing attack against another team that surrendered almost 300 yards in their last home game doesn’t sound like a good time. Any chance Jahmyr Gibbs is on vacation or enough of a Wizard of Oz style witch where he isn’t allowed to get wet?

Jahmyr Gibbs figures to be available come rain, sleet, snow, or such poor field conditions that the NFLPA has to file a grievance. 

You’re going to predict a Lions win, there’s no doubt or shame in that. The interesting question is how big of a win do you think the Lions will have and does that differ from the expectations of the broader Lions fanbase?

There’s no way Dan Campbell will have this Lions team overlooking this Panthers team, and I’m not going to either. Their passing attack is explosive, their run defense against running backs has actually been pretty solid the past two weeks, and they’re likely getting Devin Lloyd back for this one. While this one could very well become a shootout—weather permitting—it should be a more tightly contested game. It wouldn’t surprise me if the Lions win by less than one score, and it wouldn’t shock me if the Panthers pull off the upset as home underdogs coming off a disappointing loss in Week 3.

item.title: Chargers vs. Seahawks: How to watch, prediction and betting odds
item.description: Everything you need to know about the Rams facing the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, including start time, TV channel, injury updates and betting odds.
item.content:encoded:
His right arm is unquestionably superb, but does Justin Herbert have two left feet?

NFL linebacker-turned-anayst Tedy Bruschi pondered as much this week in breaking down why the relationship between the Chargers’ quarterback and offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel has yet to click.

“I want to know if Justin Herbert can dance,” the impassioned Bruschi said on ESPN. “Really, like dance on a dance floor. Does he have rhythm?”

Because, Bruschi said, quarterback Tua Tagovailoa seemed much more attuned to McDaniel’s offense when the two teamed up for the Miami Dolphins.

Read more:Mike McDaniel blames himself for Chargers' woes, remains confident of turnaround

“When Tua ran this offense, he was dancing,” Bruschi continued. “All the fakes, all the rhythmic, on time, left-handed. I mean, you would watch Tua and it was like boom, boom, boom, boom, gone [throwing an imaginary football]. He was dancing back there in the pocket. It was smoke and mirrors. That, at its best, is what this system is.

“And you’ve got a cyborg back there [in Herbert], a quarterback who can do everything under the sun, and now he has to learn to dance? ‘No, man, I don’t dance. I play football.’ So there’s just a little bit of conflict going on.”

The Chargers are 0-3 and Herbert has yet to hit his stride heading into Sunday’s game at Seattle. He has three touchdowns, four interceptions and a ho-hum passer rating of 73.4 after never finishing a season with a rating lower than 93.2. Granted, it’s early and there’s plenty of time for him to course correct, and his receivers have had several key bobbles and drops. But the schedule doesn’t get any easier soon for the Chargers, whose next games are against Denver, Kansas City, the Rams, Houston and Baltimore.

In short, the Chargers had better learn to navigate that dance floor. The night is not so young anymore.

Seahawks: RB Zach Charbonnet (knee) out; RB Jadarian Price (chest) out; S Ty Okada (hamstring) questionable; LB Chazz Surratt (calf) questionable.

The Chargers and Seattle Seahawks will play Sunday at 1:25 p.m. at Lumen Field in Seattle. The game will be shown in Southern California on CBS and Paramount+. It will be available nationally via a subscription to NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV. In Southern California, fans can listen to the game on 640 AM and 103.9 FM (Español).

Who will win Chargers vs. Seahawks?

Not great for the Chargers that the Seahawks are coming off an embarrassing loss at Washington. Seattle should be hyper-focused. Still, the Chargers can play with anyone when they’re on their game, so an upset is entirely plausible. Tough opponent, loud place, difficult stretch.

item.title: From 0-3 to the playoffs: History offers Chargers some hope for a comeback
item.description: The Chargers are searching for answers amid a winless start as they head into a showdown with the Seattle Seahawks, but their situation isn't hopeless.
item.content:encoded:
On one side there’s hope. On the other, history.

Three weeks is only a sliver of the NFL season; a backsliding team has plenty of time to correct its course.

That said, only seven teams in the Super Bowl era have rebounded from an 0-3 start to make the playoffs.

That’s a sobering statistic for the Chargers, Houston Texans and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, all winless so far. As for the 0-3 Miami Dolphins, well, that isn’t quite as shocking.

“We’re searching for every possible way to give ourselves an advantage,” said Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh, whose team lost at Buffalo last Sunday despite five takeaways and a plus-four turnover differential.

Read more:Mike McDaniel blames himself for Chargers' woes, remains confident of turnaround

The uphill climb continues for the Chargers, who play at Seattle on Sunday, with the defending Super Bowl champions itching to respond to an upset loss at Washington in Week 3.

So far, the change at offensive coordinator to former Dolphins coach Mike McDaniel has been a bust for the Chargers. Their offense has sputtered and wheezed, even as their defense has done its part to keep them in games.

Elsewhere Sunday, the Texans play host to Dallas, Tampa Bay hosts Green Bay, and Miami plays at 3-0 Minnesota.

Of those seven teams that dug themselves out of a foreboding pit, only the 1992 San Diego Chargers turned their season around after an 0-4 start — so it’s pretty much now or never for this year’s class of Sunday strugglers.

The others to make the playoffs after losing their first three games were the 1981 New York Jets, 1982 Buccaneers, 1995 Detroit Lions, 1998 Buffalo Bills, and the Texans, who pulled off the feat in 2018 and last season... and now find themselves back in that dank basement.

“We’ve been here before,” Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud told reporters this week, “so we know we can get this thing turned around.”

For those who have made that euphoric U-turn, there are life lessons to draw upon. Chief among them, don’t panic.

Former Lions linebacker Stephen Boyd recalls the composure and calm of Detroit coach Wayne Fontes, after three losses to Pittsburgh, Minnesota and Arizona — two of those by a field goal.

After the third loss, Boyd said, “Wayne Fontes walks into the meeting room with a big smile on his face and says, `Listen, here’s the deal, we’re going to give the ball to Barry [Sanders] a little bit more, and we’re going to get this turned around.’”

Sure enough, the Lions broke through the following week with a win over San Francisco on Monday night. But there were more bumps in the road for Detroit, which by November was still a dismal 3-6. Few could have predicted the club would win its final seven games.

That set the stage for a strange wild-card game against Philadelphia in which the Eagles built a 51-7 lead and held on despite the Lions scoring 30 points down the stretch. The final score: 58-37.

Three years before Fontes kept his cool under pressure, Chargers coach Bobby Ross did the same.

“There were a lot of grumblings that this was just some college coach that didn’t know what he was doing in the pros,” recalled former Chargers linebacker Gary Plummer of Ross, hired out of Georgia Tech. “There were a lot of guys that were essentially jumping off the ship.”

Read more:49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games, fined $500,000 by NFL

That team held a players-only meeting after falling to 0-3… then got clobbered, 27-0, by the Houston Oilers in Week 4.

Ross held steady, though.

“He told us that he wasn’t changing,” Plummer said. “We were still going to have physical practices. He said that was the only way he knew how to coach.”

The Chargers responded by winning four in a row. Then, after a hard-fought, two-point loss to Kansas City, the Chargers tore off another seven wins.

Defense led the way for those Chargers, allowing just 241 points that season, the fourth-fewest in the NFL.

So far this season, these Chargers are showing similar tendencies. Last Sunday, the defense played a gem of a game, and certainly through three quarters.

Hope still has a heartbeat, but that grows fainter by the loss.

item.content:encoded:
During the offseason, Rams coach Sean McVay said that receiver Davante Adams’ name came up when the Philadelphia Eagles were shopping for trade partners for receiver AJ Brown.

Adams said at the start of training camp — months after the Eagles traded Brown to the New England Patriots — that he understood that was part of the business.

The Rams are happy that Adams remains in the fold.

Heading into Sunday’s game against the Eagles, the 13th-year pro has amassed a career-best 358 receiving yards through three games.

“Fine wine gets better with time,” offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase said.

Read more:Rams' Puka Nacua 'smiling' over the thought of playing the Eagles

Adams, 33, is coming off two consecutive 100-yard receiving performances.

With receiver Puka Nacua sidelined because of a hip injury, Adams caught eight passes for 195 yards and two touchdowns in a 28-6 victory over the New York Giants, and he had seven receptions for 137 yards in a 30-26 defeat by the Denver Broncos.

“I don’t necessarily need a 100-yard game to validate what I can do on the field,” said Adams, who is in his second season with the Rams. “Coming to a team like this where you have playmakers literally at every single position, it’s not necessary.

“If it is necessary and I’m called on, then I’ll go and answer the bell on that. Whatever my game or my role looks like for whatever the situation is, I try to live up to that.”

Adams is tied for the league lead with nine catches of 15 yards or more.

Asked if he was conscious that after catching passes in space at 33, he might not get to a faraway end zone as quickly as he did in his 20s, Adams had a good-natured response.

Adams said he has never been looked at in the same way as “a burner” such as Tyreek Hill. But he makes the most of speed and experience.

“When I see an open field, I’m running, obviously, as hard as I can to get to the end zone and try to score any time that I can,” he said. “Angles and certain things obviously influence whether or not you can get in. I don’t have a whole lot of 91-yard touchdowns in my career so I don’t know if I would have got in as a 24 or 23-year-old.

“When I see that space, I’m always pushing to get there. I’m running as hard as I can without pulling any ‘hammies’ [hamstrings] or doing anything crazy out there.”

Nacua, the NFL receptions leader last season, will return to the lineup against the Eagles. Nacua and other Rams receivers continue to be awed by Adams after his back-to-back 100-yard performances.

“It’s funny because with him being the veteran in our group and quote-unquote ‘the old guy,’ it’s been really exciting for him,” Nacua said. “There’s a breath of fresh air that I think we bring to him, but also that standard where he’s as competitive as it comes.”

item.title: Amarius Mims draws strong praise from offensive line guru
item.description: The Bengals once again have a dominant right tackle.
item.content:encoded:
If there was a true bright spot that has been consistent throughout the season so far for the Cincinnati Bengals, it would be right tackle Amarius Mims playing practically perfect.

Mims has shut down every pass rusher he has gone against so far. That list includes the likes of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter from the Houston Texans.

It also includes T.J. Watt from the game on Sunday with the Pittsburgh Steelers. That performance caught the eye of Brandon Thorn — one of the best offensive linemen evaluators — who has high praise after Mims incredible start, calling him a top 5-to-6 right tackle in the NFL.

“This is a top 5-6 RT in just his 3rd season,” said Thorn.

The knock on Mims during the draft process was that he couldn’t stay healthy. That always seemed unfounded considering he never even had a major knee injury. Just some moderate to minor injuries that popped up near the end of his time in college and during the draft process itself. It also created a lack-of-experience concern, but he never had an issue in the SEC.

That’s why the Bengals may have gotten the steal of the draft at No. 18 overall in the 2024 NFL Draft. He has hit what many called his high ceiling of potential. Those kinds of picks haven’t always worked out, but it is clear they nailed this one if Mims can stay healthy.

The only question that comes now is if he eventually gets moved to left tackle. Orlando Brown Jr. has struggled a bit with some of the quicker rushers in the NFL, and it has showed up quite a few times over the years, but he is far from being an unacceptable starter. It may come down to whether they feel the move can be made, and how much exactly they end up having to pay him when that contract needs to be redone. Because he surely should push for elite tackle money, but left tackle will always get more in that area.

That is a long-term discussion, though. We get to enjoy him as an absolute dominant offensive tackle right now.

item.title: Patriots worried about ‘second play’ with Bills QB Josh Allen
item.description: Buffalo’s quarterback is presenting all sorts of problems for the Patriots defense.
item.content:encoded:
Josh Allen’s status as one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL is undisputed. What makes him such a dangerous and productive player is not just his arm talent, size and versatility, but how he uses a combination of his rare skills to become arguably the most frustration-inducing player in all of pro football.

As long as he has the ball, after all, the Buffalo Bills have a chance. And the 30-year-old is making sure to keep that chance alive for as long as he can on every single play.

This, in turn, puts immense pressure on opponents to keep defending even when a play otherwise would be long over. It is precisely what the New England Patriots have been harping on all week.

“He’s going to extend plays. We know that’s going to happen. You can’t necessarily stop it, you only can contain it,” said safety Kevin Byard.

“As DBs, we have to be able to cover for as long as it takes. Ten seconds — it doesn’t matter. Especially on the backend, it’s not necessarily the play that’s called, it’s the second or third play within the play. So, we’re going to have to be very mentally, but more than likely physically exhausted in this game because this team and Josh, they have no quit.”

Defending the “second play” has been the Patriots’ defensive theme of the week. On the flip side, making said play has been Allen’s bread and butter since entering the NFL as a first-round draft choice out of Wyoming in 2018.

“It’s kind of like recess football in terms of, ‘If you have a man, you have to cover your man. And if you’re free, then you have to figure out a way to get this guy with the ball either down or out of bounds,’” said Patriots cornerbacks coach Justin Hamilton. “He’s elite, and he’s as good as I can remember seeing in my lifetime. I’ve watched a lot of NFL football. I don’t know of a guy that’s better at play extension.”

Allen is able to make the so-called second plays because of his size, strength and vision. He can simply evade pressure or fight through tackle attempts, all while keeping his eyes downfield for either a rushing lane or receiver to open up downfield. This is why he is typically ranked high in time-to-throw metrics and also one of the most effective scrambling quarterbacks in the league.

None of that is nothing new, of course. Defending it still remains a challenge, though — one the Patriots are going up against twice a year, including this coming Sunday.

“It’s the hardest thing, in my opinion, in football to have to defend,” said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr, who referred to Allen as an “MVP-caliber quarterback playing MVP football.”

For him, the secret to countering the extended play lies in the preparation. The goal is not just to know what is going to happen, but be capable of reacting in an instant without much hesitation.

Kuhr used two words to describe the approach: muscle memory.

“We try to rep it in practice. Tommy [DeVito] and Behren [Morton] are giving good looks,” he said. “We talk about our rules within it and we harp on it every single day, we show the film of it. Everybody’s got to know it. Everybody’s got to be on the same page. Everybody’s got to understand it, so it becomes muscle memory because he’s a special cat and he’s a different cat. You know you get to see that twice a year and it just looks different, so we have to do everything we can to make how we execute the second play muscle memory.

“There can’t be any lapses of, ‘I thought the play was over.’ No, the play is never over. We have to do it for 60 minutes too — that’s the hardest part: this guy does not go away. No matter what the score is, he does not go away. So, we have to have the competitive stamina for 60 minutes, understand what our rules are to defend the second play, and we all have to be on the same page doing it, make it muscle memory.”

Muscle memory is one part, game-day execution another. And for the Patriots, the latter will be difficult this week given their personnel situation.

Two of their best defenders, cornerback Christian Gonzalez and defensive tackle Christian Barmore, will miss the contest on Sunday due to shoulder injuries. Under normal circumstances both would play valuable roles in keeping Allen contained through tight coverage and resetting the line of scrimmage, respectively.

Without those blue-chip players, the task will be even more daunting than it already is.

“It’s going to be a 60-minute ball game,” said Byard. “We could be up 35 points and he’s going to find a way to try to come back and score 40 points. This is going to be a tough challenge for us and we’re going to have to play a 60-minute complete ball game.”

item.description: Head Coach Sean Payton had high praise for the coaching staff of the San Francisco 49ers.
item.content:encoded:
After decades of coaching in the National Football League, Denver Broncos Head Coach Sean Payton has seen a lot of coaches come and go. During his time with the New Orleans Saints in the NFC South—Payton became quite familiar with Kyle Shanahan and Raheem Morris—who will be leading the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday.

Those two men, as well as a quality roster of players, stand in the way of the Broncos’ pursuit of third straight victory. Under their guidance, the 49ers are undefeated to start their 2026 season. San Francisco sports both a Top 5 offense and defense and appear to be a championship caliber squad. Yesterday after practice, Payton had a lot of praise for Shanahan, who is in his tenth season leading the 49ers.

“There are so many things he does well. He—like his father—it started with an elite run-game plan. That hasn’t changed. Some of the play-actions that come off of that run game, I can recall snaps in Atlanta where Matt Ryan is extending the ball, and then all of the sudden pulls it up, and you look down the field and there’s somebody wide open,” recalled Payton with respect to memories of Shanahan over the years.

“That’s just one element of what makes him special. I think that balance relative to run and pass. We had a number of years together in the division, and then over the years as he’s become a head coach and you’re at Owners Meetings and Combines. I’m close with his father. We have a great relationship.”

Shanahan has done well calling plays and leading the 49ers’ offense. They are near the top of the league in points scored and have been incredible on third down and in the red zone. When it matters most, Shanahan’s players have been executing at a high level.

As Payton mentioned, the running game is front and center of Shanahan’s offensive game plans. This year, they have one of the best ground games in the NFL with Christian McCaffrey and rookie third-round pick Kaelon Black. If Denver hopes to win on the road, they can’t let McCaffrey and Black run wild over their defense.

On top of that, their passing offense has been incredibly efficient too. Bringing back Deebo Samuel was a good choice by their front office. Moreover, adding Mike Evans at wide receiver has really opened things up for fifth-year quarterback Brock Purdy in the passing game. Purdy leads the NFL with 9 touchdowns and only one interception and has yet to be sacked through three games.

What Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph has in store to contain the 49ers’ high-powered offense is anyone’s best guess. Without question, it will certainly be quite the chess-match for Joseph, who has had his fair share of battles against Shanahan over the years.

On offense, the Broncos are still trying to find their way. They’ve looked much better in the second half in their back-to-back comeback victories. Unfortunately, their overall efficiency and productivity have been hampered by slow starts.

Denver hasn’t been able to run the ball well consistently, are struggling converting third downs, and have had too many penalties and turnovers early on in games. It’s not a recipe for success and something the Broncos will have to figure out in short order to be top-tier competitors the rest of the season.

This Sunday, Payton and Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb hope to establish an operable game plan that can combat one of the league’s best defenses coached by Morris. The 49ers allowed just 20 points in their first two contests but had issues stopping the run and getting pressure in their Week 3 win against the Cardinals.

“He’s done a real good job defensively. They’re playing real good red-zone defense. They present a lot of problems,” remarked Payton.

“There’s so much more film that we’re all looking at. We all see it. The defense was different. This goes all the way back to when he was at Tampa. I’ve known Raheem for ages. Joint practice here with the Rams. He was in Atlanta. He’s a tremendous coach with great juice,” added Payton.

Sunday’s matchup will be a huge test for the Broncos. The 49ers a well-coached team with a roster stacked with quality players all across the board. In order to achieve a victory, Payton and his staff are going to be at their best. Which coaching staff will come up with the better game plan? You’ll just have to tune in and find out.

item.title: NY Giants news: Malik Nabers, J.J. McCarthy, more
item.description: New York Giants headlines for Saturday
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about as the Giants look to stay atop the NFC East with a win this Sunday.

NFL Week 4 preview | ESPN.com

The Giants seem to know they’re not facing the Titans’ offense again this week. It was mentioned several times that the Cardinals are “very similar” offensively to the Rams — who dismantled the Giants two weeks ago — which DC Dennard Wilson noted because of Arizona coach Mike LaFleur’s ties to Sean McVay. New York knows it’s going to be a difficult challenge, particularly stopping rookie RB Jeremiyah Love, who it had ranked as a top-three player in the 2026 draft.

Can Jameis Winston hold off JJ McCarthy? Where’s the pass rush? What to watch for in Giants-Cardinals | The Athletic

A weak Arizona Cardinals pass defense should provide the streaky Winston an opportunity to find his groove. But if Winston struggles again and the Giants lose, the focus immediately will shift to his job security. A key variable will be how quickly McCarthy learns the offense. He only has 10 career starts and the Giants’ offense puts a lot on the quarterback’s plate. Rushing McCarthy into action before he’s ready would be a huge mistake. But there’s an understanding that McCarthy won’t be able to fully get up to speed on the offense midstream.

With an upcoming stretch against the 1-2 Cardinals, the 1-2 Commanders, the 1-2 Saints and the 0-3 Texans, the Giants’ best bet to building momentum is Winston turning things around. If the 2-1 Giants can’t string some wins together now, it will be asking a lot for McCarthy to save the season when the schedule stiffens after their Week 8 bye.

New Giants QB candid about if he can thrive amid fresh start: ‘Nobody knows’ | NJ.com

McCarthy said he’s attacking the new offense day-by-day, but said he feels he’s picking it up pretty quickly. When asked how close he is to being ready to go into a game, McCarthy said, “At the end of the day, I’m just focused on watching this practice, learning from it and making sure I get this game plan down. I’m really just focused on being in the present moment and going from there.”

McCarthy wasn’t interested in dwelling on what went wrong in Minnesota. “There’s a multitude of things you can think of, but at the end of the day, it’s all in the past,” he said. “All I care about is what’s important now — that next rep, that next meeting, that next game. That’s really all I’m focused on.”

Giants rookie Colton Hood ‘baptized by fire’ by intense NFL initiation | New York Post

Initiations into the NFL don’t get any more difficult than defending Matthew Stafford throwing to Davante Adams in your first career start. But Hood also allowed Wan’Dale Robinson’s touchdown last game.  Hood has allowed 11 catches on 15 targets for 106 yards and two touchdowns over three games, according to NextGenStats. Opposing quarterbacks have a 132.2 rating when throwing at him. 

“I’m encouraged by, just watching the film, none of it is, ‘This guy is just better than me and beat me,’ ” Hood told The Post. “It’s more just seeing things for the first time and processing things post-snap. It’s just that I’m at a different level and learning how to combat those things. The routes in the league are different, you have to adjust to the depth. And the coverages, you have to understand not just your job but the people around you’s job so you can play tighter.” 

Rush to judgment as Giants defense promises to crank things up on QBs | The Record

The New York Giants have looked in the mirror. They’ve studied the tape and scoured the stat sheet, only to be left incredibly disappointed with what they have seen.

DC Dennard Wilson thinks Jihad Ward can be ‘good factor’ in Giants defense | SNY.tv

Ward appeared in all 17 of Tennessee’s games (starting 12 of them) and he recorded career-highs in defensive snaps (708), quarterback hits (22), and sacks (5.0). 

“Haddy is a guy that played extremely well for me,” Wilson said. “He brings versatility to play on the edge, he brings versatility to play in the middle of the defense if we need, and he can be an interior rusher if we need, too. Haddy’s going to be ready when his number is called. We’ll see how it plays out from today going forward to Sunday and the weeks after that — but he’s an ultimate professional, and he’s going to be prepared.  He’s been in camp with the Vikings, he’s in shape, so we’ll see how the chips fall here — I feel that Haddy could be a good factor in our defense moving forward.”

Scouts: Giants Unlikely To Find Buried Treasure In McCarthy | FOX Sports

“There’s no doubt McCarthy has talent,” one scout told me. “He’s probably a good fit for what they want to do, too. But honestly, if the Vikings were willing to dump their one-time franchise quarterback for a fifth-round pick, you really got to wonder what they know. Teams don’t usually dump young quarterbacks like that, especially ones they took 10th overall.”

“Think about that,” one NFL assistant told me. “He couldn’t beat out Murray or Wentz. That doesn’t happen to a high first-round pick. That’s what happens with late-round and practice squad-type guys. So that tells you everything about what Minnesota thinks of him. Maybe a change of scenery will help. But O’Connell is pretty good with quarterbacks. If he couldn’t get anything out of the kid, I don’t know if anyone on the Giants can.”

item.title: Did the offense, defense, or Dan Quinn win it for Washington? Fans weigh in after the Seattle upset - survey results
item.description: 3 defensive takeaways, clutch drives, and good accuracy from the rookie kicker prove nobody carried Washington alone in Sunday’s upset win over the Seahawks
item.content:encoded:
Sunday’s 33-31 upset over the Seattle Seahawks did a lot more than just put a mark in the win column. It gave Commanders fans a collective sigh of relief and brought back an energy that seemed completely sapped just seven days earlier.

In this week’s Reacts survey, we dug into two key areas: our regular check-in on fan confidence, and an evaluation of which unit deserved the lion’s share of the credit for pulling off the home upset.

Here is how the votes shook out and what our community had to say.

Question 1: Are you confident in the team’s direction?

The rollercoaster ride continues.

After opening at 70% in Week 1 and ticking up to 80% following Week 2, the bottom fell out in Week 3 at a dismal 20%. One week and one signature upset later, that number has bounced right back up to 76%.

Whether this jump represents genuine long-term faith or simply immediate postgame relief following the win in the home opener vs the Seashawks, the mood around the fanbase has clearly turned back toward the positive.

Still, a few regular commenters were quick to separate game-day emotion from long-term trajectory.

Others are keeping their guard up.

By the way, here are this week’s results of the confidence question from the other NFC East teams:

Question 2: Which phase of the game was most instrumental in the Commanders win over the Seahawks on Sunday?

Visit our partners at FanDuel

Nearly half the votes went to the offense with just over a third to defense, but reading through the comments, our community wasn’t ready to let David Blough take a solo victory lap.

Defense: The reality is that Sunday was a clinic in complementary football. Daronte Jones’ defense repeatedly bailed out the team by clamping down on Seattle’s ground attack and generating 3 critical takeaways—none bigger than the second-half pick-six that completely flipped momentum.

Offense: At the same time, when Blough’s offense had to have a drive in the fourth quarter, Marcus Mariota settled down, shook off that rough 1-for-11 third-down mark, and led a clutch scoring march that drained the clock and sealed the win.

Special Teams: Then there is the third phase that often gets forgotten: special teams. In a game decided by just 2 points, rookie kicker Drew Stevens was dead-eye reliable on 3-pointers. He nailed both of his field goal tries under immense pressure (we won’t talk about the missed 48-yard PAT following the penalty on Frankie Luvu, who wasn’t even playing in the game). Without Stevens doing his field-goal kicking job cleanly, all the defensive takeaways in the world might not have been enough.

DQ: The 19% of respondents who gave their vote to Dan Quinn probably may have been onto something: nobody carried this team across the finish line alone. When a team plays together and comes away with a win in difficult circumstances, the head coach has to get some credit for that, right?

Wrapping up the thought
When a squad is banged up and leaning on backups in critical spots, winning doesn’t come down to a single playcaller having a stroke of genius. It requires all three phases covering for one another when things go sideways. Daronte Jones’ defense provided the short fields and the splash plays, David Blough’s offense capitalized with a clutch, clock-killing touchdown drive when it mattered most, and Drew Stevens quietly put 6 points on the board to make sure no offensive drives that crossed midfield prior to the 2-minute warning were wasted. That is textbook complementary football, and fostering that kind of buy-in across the roster is ultimately the head coach’s job.

Next up: a Week 4 international showdown in London against Daniel Jones and the Indianapolis Colts

Holding onto the team’s collective resilience will be vital as Washington packs its bags for London. With a quick turnaround, international travel logistics, and an Indianapolis team eager to turn Daniel Jones loose against his old NFC East rival, the Commanders won’t have the luxury of relying on just one side of the ball. If Sunday proved anything, it’s that this team’s margin for error is razor-thin—and their best chance to keep stacking wins is by doing it together.

Per Fan Duel, Indianapolis is currently favored on Sunday.

  • Colts -3.5
  • Over/under 47.5

The game will be played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Sunday, October 4, with kickoff slated for an early 9:30 a.m. EDT (2:30 p.m. local BST) on NFL Network.

So, set those morning alarms early, grab a pot of coffee, and get ready for Sunday brunch with the burgundy & gold!
