item.description: Your daily San Francisco 49ers news for Saturday, October 3rd, 2026
item.content:encoded:
What will we learn about this team from this match-up? The Broncos are like a scaled-down version of some of the beasts they’d need to slay on their way to the Super Bowl. A legit defensive line (but not quite Seattle), an athletic quarterback (but not quite a peak Mahomes or Josh Allen), and a veteran coach on Kyle’s level (but not quite Andy Reid). This almost feels like the starting gun to the “real” season. Here are the things I will be looking for, beyond the box score, that can tell us a lot about this team… 

Can the 49ers handle a ferocious pass rush? It’s great that the offensive line hasn’t given up a sack. They haven’t faced a defensive line this good yet. Seattle next week will be even better. Connor Colby and the interior o-line have exceeded my expectations so far, but this isn’t Miami or Arizona. 

Can the 49ers keep exploiting linebackers in coverage without their best wide receivers? Mike Evans might not play. All due respect to Brandin Cooks, but they need big games out of their non-WR skill players like George Kittle, Christian McCaffrey, and even a little Kyle Jusczyzk. That’s always been the case but especially so against the “elite DB/vulnerable LB” combination that Denver has going. 

Can the 49ers establish the run? Kansas City provided the blueprint in Week 1 when they forced the Broncos to miss 26 tackles. 

Can they keep an athletic quarterback in the pocket…. without Nick Bosa? Bo Nix isn’t as good as Matt Stafford but he is the most athletic QB they’ve faced yet (that’s still a mid-tier or above passer). He’s maddenly inconsistent but can also win games on his own. 

How’s the secondary holding up? Jaylen Waddle is good to go, and Courtland Sutton is no slouch. I can see a world where the Broncos start slow and then start coming back because of coverage busts on the back end. It just takes one bad bust to breathe life into Bo Nix, who otherwise struggles when forced to step up in the pocket. 

Wait, is the 49ers O-line actually good? Broncos, Seahawks can help settle the debate (paywall)
“Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said the big red zone sack Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga had against the Los Angeles Rams late in Denver’s win Sunday shows how efficient — and aggressive — defensive coordinator Vance Joseph’s unit can be. Hufanga, a former 49er, lined up to quarterback Matthew Stafford’s blind side at the last second and was unaccounted for as he came off the edge.

“He knows when to call his shots,” Kubiak said of Joseph. “He knows when to be aggressive and come after the quarterback. That group’s been playing together for a while. And when they call those blitzes, they usually work.”

Part of the 49ers’ winning formula so far this year is that they aren’t hurting themselves.”

Five 49ers to watch as Brock Purdy leads charge to stay undefeated vs. Broncos
“Defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa clearly is the main guy. The 49ers need another player or two to stand out among their nine-man rotation. Rookie Gracen Halton could be on the verge of a breakout.

Halton, a fourth-round 2026 NFL Draft pick, will make his third start in a row. He has a couple of tackles for loss, and appears to be trending toward making more big plays.”

49ers add a rookie to the injury report; Dante Pettis hurt his calf
“Evans will be a game-time decision with his rib injury. Shanahan compared his rib injury to Evans, saying, “he’s definitely a lot tougher than me. Hopefully, he’s got a shot.”

Brandin Cooks will make his 49ers debut on Sunday.”

49ers vs. Broncos: The Standard’s 5 fast predictions (paywall)
“Kawakami: Broncos 27, 49ers 26. This would be a disappointing way for the 49ers to go into next weekend’s clash in Seattle. But they’re probably due for a flat performance perhaps with some natural focus on the flight to the Northwest coming up. Also, any more Eddy Piñeiro extra-point misses could be huge in a close game.”

Kyle Shanahan shares final updates ahead of 49ers-Broncos
“When you’re talking to your team about an upcoming opponent, do you find yourself have to talk up the opponent more or do you want to build your team’s confidence or appropriate fear? How do you approach it?

“All of the above. Depends where we’re at at the time, where the team’s at. It changes every week. You can have it come off a huge win and people question the team you’re playing. That happened to us in Week Two. A big win versus the Rams in Australia. Then people have us as huge favorites and stuff the next week versus Miami. I don’t try to talk people up because I don’t think people believe words. I think people believe what they see and I can’t talk people up unless I believe it. So, I usually try to find it in the tape and show people what people can be and what they need to be worried about. It’s something I usually do earlier in the week. I think that fear to fail or respect of people, however you want to word it, is what gets you to work a certain way. The whole goal is to work hard enough so you don’t feel that way, and to me, the goal is to not feel that way by Saturday night so you go into Sunday confident. And if you feel that way on Monday, I usually think you’re in trouble. You’ve got to earn that. It’s got to be real, and that’s through the work you do and the preparation. You prepare the right way if you respect an opponent and I believe we respect whoever we’re playing every week.”

item.title: Eagles notebook: A key area to improve on defense
item.description: In the latest Eagles notebook, the need for more communication on defense, Jalen Carter's wrist injury and more.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles notebook: A key area to improve on defense originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Eagles’ secondary looked a bit lost on Monday night in Chicago as they allowed Case Keenum to throw for 247 yards and 2 touchdowns in an embarrassing loss.

Cooper DeJean this week said he knows what has to change.

They need to communicate better.

“I think our biggest thing right now is just there’s not enough talking on the field between everybody, myself included,” DeJean said. “To the corners, to the safeties, linebackers, everybody just needs to communicate a little bit more so we’re all on the same page. We made too many mistakes that were unforced, that shouldn’t happen, that are easy things that we’ve repped many times. We just have to communicate better.”

While Fangio pointed at just the 41-yard touchdown pass in the third quarter as an example of miscommunication, DeJean said there were multiple moments where the communication wasn’t up to their standard.

How do the Eagles start to fix the problem?

“It starts at practice,” DeJean said. “Just communicate more, make sure everybody is talking every single snap. A lot of guys in this defense. Communication is key. There’s a lot of moving parts so you gotta make sure everybody is on the same page.”

The Eagles brought back many players from their 2025 season but there are some new faces too. This Eagles defense also doesn’t have Nakobe Dean or Reed Blankenship and DeJean admitted that’s hurting the communication “maybe a little.”

“We just have to be confident in what we call out there on the field,” DeJean said. “As long as everybody is playing the same call, we’ll be good. The biggest thing is just getting everybody on the same page. That starts with communication with everybody.”

Playing through injury

For the last couple of weeks, Jalen Carter has been wearing a cast on his right hand because of a hairline fracture in his wrist. And it has clearly affected his play.

Carter, 25, said he tries not to let the cast affect him and avoids excuses. But hand usage for defensive linemen is so important.

“You got to use your hands as a D-lineman every play, every snap and all that,” Carter said. “It’s a bit impact when you can’t really use everything with striking, pulling off transition to pass, etc. But you just have to work through it. Some people don’t even got the ability to have their fingers out. Some people just got the full club.”

The Eagles this offseason gave Carter a massive four-year, $152 million extension that made him the highest paid DT in the NFL. Because of this injury, though, he hasn’t been able to live up to that just yet.

Earlier this week, even defensive coordinator Vic Fangio admitted the injury has negatively affected Carter, who played just 71% of the Eagles’ defensive snaps on Monday night — a low percentage for him.

The good news is that Carter estimates he will only have to wear that case for “probably a couple more weeks” and he said the strength in that wrist is already starting to return.

“I’m hoping to be able to take it off,” Carter said. “I’m not planning on wearing it through the whole season.”

Sticking with 11 personnel

As much of the NFL is starting to lean heavily into multiple tight end sets, the Eagles have gone the other way. They have been in their 11 personnel package (3 receivers) for 76.7% of their snaps this season.

That’s the highest percentage in the NFL, ahead of the Titans (72.0%), Saints (70.3%), Panthers (67.4%) and Cowboys (67.2%).

This seems to have a lot to do with the Eagles’ lack of depth at tight end, especially after the Dallas Goedert injury. Eagles OC Sean Mannion said there are multiple factors that have contributed to this.

“You’re managing injuries throughout the week, you’re managing the opponent and their tendencies, what they may be doing with their personnel and how you want to attack that specifically,” Mannion said. “There’s a couple of factors there. Obviously, it’s a shame Dallas got dinged up in that Tennessee game. He’s a big part of what we’re doing, but we have a lot of good depth there. I know Zach (Ertz) came in on short notice and filled a good role for us. We love what we have out of E.J. (Jenkins) and Johnny (Mundt).

“I really like that group, really like the receiver group. It’s a luxury for us that we feel we have the flexibility to do multiple things based on the opponent and based on whatever situation we have going on with our personnel. Some of it’s injury, some of it’s the opponent. I guess to answer your question, it’s a little bit of both week to week.”

Dealing with the Rams

The Eagles’ defense got shredded by the Bears on Monday night and things won’t be any easier in Week 4.

The Rams have the NFL’s No. 1 ranked offense, averaging 417.7 yards per game. This is a high-flying attack that is very balanced.

“Yeah, they’re really good,” defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said. “Not counting their San Francisco game in Australia, their last three games going back to the NFC Championship Game, they’ve gotten 500 yards in all three games against Seattle, the Giants and Denver. Three good defenses. That in and of itself explains to you what the chore is we have. 

“They run it very well. They stay committed to the run and they’ve got a really good play action game off of it that they marry very well to the run game. You’ve got (Matthew) Stafford at quarterback, guy’s going to be a first ballot Hall of Famer. Got the weapons and the tight ends that they have and they’re probably having the (Puka) Nacua back this week. So yeah, it’s a tough assignment because they’re balanced and they run and throw it very effectively.”

The Rams had 481 yards against the Giants in Week 2 and 482 yards against the Broncos in Week 3. They’re the only team in the NFL to have back-to-back 480+ yard games so far this season.

Age over beauty 

The Eagles lost to 38-year-old Case Keenum in Week 3 and they’ll face another 38-year-old quarterback in Matthew Stafford in Week 4.

This is the first time in franchise history the Eagles are facing 38+ year-old QBs in back-to-back weeks. And the old guys have performed well against them. Since 2018, the Eagles have faced a QB who is 38 or older eight times and are 2-6 against them with losses to Keenum, Josh Johnson, Tom Brady (twice), Ben Roethlisberger and Drew Brees. The Eagles’ wins in that span have come over Aaron Rodgers and Eli Manning.

item.title: Roob's 10 Observations: Why we all need to be patient with Jihaad Campbell
item.description: Campbell is 22 and the third-youngest starting inside linebacker in the NFL.
item.content:encoded:
Roob's 10 Observations: Why we all need to be patient with Jihaad Campbell originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Why it would be a mistake to give up on Jihaad Campbell. What the offensive line should look like if Landon Dickerson comes back healthy. And a look back at the strange and remarkable career of Pete Pihos, one of only three Hall of Famers who spent his entire career with the Eagles.

That’s just a small sampling of the wonders that await you in this week’s edition of Roob’s 10 Random Eagles Observations.

DON’T GIVE UP ON JIHAAD CAMPBELL: I get that people are down on Jihaad Campbell right now, and some of the criticism is fair. He hasn’t been great and is not playing like a 1st-round pick, Nakobe Dean is having an all-pro season with the Raiders and it’s impossible not to compare the two since their careers will always be inexorably linked. Drafting Campbell in the first round is why the Eagles couldn’t keep Dean. But a couple things to remember: Campbell is 22 and the 3rd-youngest starting inside linebacker in the NFL. He was considered a steal where the Eagles drafted him last year at No. 31. And he hasn’t been awful. Out of 61 linebackers who’ve played at least 100 snaps, he ranks 23rd in Pro Football Focus with his overall grade, 26th in run defense and 25th in coverage, so a bit above middle of the pack in every category. He hasn’t covered as well as you’d expect, but it’s way too early to even think about calling him a 1st-round bust. He’s a young guy with great size and athleticism, and there’s no reason to think he won’t get better working under ace linebackers coach Bobby King. Remember, when the Eagles drafted Campbell there were significant questions about Dean as he rehabbed a severe knee injury. And he really didn’t blossom as a player until last year, after Campbell was already here. Campbell is the youngest Eagles starting linebacker ever, and he’s the 2nd-youngest defensive player in franchise history to start double-digit games, just a bit older than 1950s defensive tackle Ernie Calloway. Good ol’ Ernie. Maybe Campbell won’t work out. Maybe he won’t pan out as a top-tier linebacker. Maybe a rare Howie miss. Maybe Jeremiah Trotter will play so well against the Rams Sunday Vic Fangio will be tempted to make a switch once Zack Baun is back. But it’s too early to give up hope. Let’s see where Campbell is at the end of this year and even into next year before we write him off. I still think he has a chance to be a player.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN LANDON DICKERSON COMES BACK? Who knows when or if Landon Dickerson will come back healthy. He’ll be eligible to come off Injured Reserve after next week’s London game against the Jaguars, but we’ll see if that happens. But if he does come back and is able to play at something approaching his three-time Pro Bowl level, what’s next for the Eagles’ offensive line? I’m not sure Nick Sirianni would do it, but Dickerson should probably replace Cam Jurgens at left guard, with Drew Kendall staying at center. Kendall was very good Monday night in Chicago – Pro Football Focus had him as the highest-rated center in the league in Week 4 – while Jurgens has continued to struggle after moving from center to left guard. If you want to get your five-best guys out there, it could very well be Dickerson and Kendall at left guard and center. And while we’re moving o-line pieces around, Tyler Steen has had a disappointing start to the season and I wonder if we’ll see Willie Lampkin out there at right guard at some point. He’s never played a regular-season snap on offense, but he was so good in training camp I wouldn’t mind seeing him get a shot. It’s possible the Eagles’ strongest offensive line is Mailata > Dickerson > Kendall > Lampkin > Johnson. But of course it’s all dependent on Dickerson coming back healthy and effective. And who knows about that. I know one thing: Whoever’s out there this o-line has to be better if the Eagles are going to return to respectability on offense.

NEGATIVE PLAYS: Along those lines, the Eagles have had 23 plays of negative yards, most in the NFL (not including kneeldowns). But they’ve only forced 13 plays of negative yards, tied for 21st-most. The 10-play differential – 13 negative plays forced, 23 run – is tied for largest in the league with the Colts, who have had 19 negative plays and allowed nine. 

FIRST HALF, SECOND HALF: Whatever the Eagles are doing at halftime, it has to change. Because their offense is one of the best in the NFL before halftime and one of the worst after halftime. The numbers honestly are shocking:
– The Eagles are averaging 4.9 yards per play in the first half, 5th-highest in the league. They’ve scored five touchdowns and they’re 4th-best on third down at 55 percent.
– Second half? Those figures go down to 3.5 yards per play (29th in the league), two touchdowns (2nd-worst) and 38 percent on third down (19th).
– The numbers are similar on the other side of the ball. The Eagles’ defense in the first half is holding teams to 3.5 yards per play (6th-best), three touchdowns (tied for 6th-best) and 36 percent on third down (10th-best) in the first half.
– Second half looks like this: 4.9 yards per play (tied for 21st), five TDs (tied for 5th-most) and 42 percent on third down (22nd).
It all adds up to getting outscored 40-20 in the second half, and that 20-point margin is their worst through three games since 1986, and they’re being outgained by an average of 188-111 after halftime. People are clearly figuring out what is working and adjusting and the Eagles aren’t adjusting back. That’s got to change now.

THE ODD CAREER OF PETE PIHOS: Pete Pihos had one of the stranger career arcs in Eagles history. In his first six seasons, 1947 through 1952, Pihos averaged 31 catches, 472 yards and 5 ½ touchdowns per season. Not bad but certainly not superstar caliber. He turned 30 early in the 1953 season and played just three more years, averaging 62 catches, 928 yards and 9.0 touchdowns, leading the NFL in catches all three years, in yards in 1953 and 1955 and in TD catches in 1953. He led the NFL during that three-year span in all three categories and made 1st-team all-pro all three years. To this day, Pihos is the only player in Eagles history with three seasons with 60 catches in his 30s. Then he abruptly retired after another 1st-team all-pro season. Pihos and Jason Kelce are the only Eagles to make 1st-team all-pro at least three times after turning 30 (Kelce did six times) and they’re among just 14 players in NFL history to make 1st-team all-pro in each of their last three seasons. Pihos retired after leading the NFL in catches and yards, citing advice he once received from Joe DiMaggio to retire at his peak so people would remember him at his best. Pihos was inducted into the Pro Bowl Hall of Fame in 1970. Along with Steve Van Buren and Chuck Bednarik, he’s one of just three Hall of Famers who spent his entire career with the Eagles. That number will increase to four in 2029 when Kelce goes in.

JALEN HURTS STAT OF THE WEEK: Hurts has accounted for more combined touchdowns in his first 85 starts than any other 2nd-round pick in NFL history. In his first 85 starts, Hurts has thrown 114 touchdown passes and run for 64 more for a total of 178. Next-most among 2nd-round picks in their first 85 starts are Brett Favre (172), Randall Cunningham (149), Andy Dalton (149), Boomer Esiason (141), Derek Carr (134), Tobin Rote (130), Drew Brees (128) and Ken Stabler (127). 

WAITING FOR A PICK: Eagles defensive backs have faced 632 passes in 20 regular-season games since opening day last year and have six interceptions – two by Drew Mukuba, two by Cooper DeJean and one each by Adoree’ Jackson and Reed Blankenship. The only teams whose d-backs have fewer interceptions since last year are the Cowboys and Titans with five apiece. The Eagles have faced 96 passes since their last interception, by Jalyx Hunt off Josh Johnson in the second quarter of the Eagles-Commanders game on the last day of last season.

THE ELUSIVE 400-YARD PLATEAU: The Eagles netted 400 yards from scrimmage 29 times in Nick Sirianni’s first 75 games as a head coach. They’ve reached 400 yards just once in their last 22 games and not at all in their last 13 games, their longest streak of games without 400 yards since 15 in a row over the 2002 and 2003 seasons. Amazingly, five teams currently have longer streaks without 400 yards: The Dolphins (36), Titans (29), Raiders (25), Vikings (21) and Bucs (15). The NFL record is 104 straight games by the Giants over the 1973 through 1980 seasons. The Eagles’ record is 57 in a row from 1969 through 1973. 

WHO’S GOING TO CATCH PASSES? With both DeVonta Smith and Hollywood Brown out for the Rams, it will be interesting to see how the Eagles line up their receivers. Dontayvion Wicks is the next outside guy, with Makai Lemon, Elijah Moore and Darius Cooper all avaiable. Of that group, Lemon has played mainly in the slot (80 snaps inside, 36 outside), Cooper is about 50-50 (22 inside, 20 outside) and Moore in his brief playing time has been inside (4 snaps) more than outside (2). Someone has to give the Eagles good outside snaps, and Cooper seems best suited for that. He’s ideally a slot, but I would expect Lemon stays in the slot with Cooper getting most of his snaps outside because he seems comfortable doing either. I wouldn’t be shocked if Britain Covey gets a handful of slot reps as well. However you line ‘em up, losing DeVonta is a huge blow. 

“GREG BELL, MY ASS:” Whenever the Eagles and Rams play, I can’t help think about Buddy Ryan’s press conference a few days before the Eagles-Rams playoff game in 1989. Because of snow and cold weather in Philly, the Eagles practiced that week at the Falcons’ facility in Suwanee, Ga., and that’s where Ryan spoke to the media at a podium in a small room in advance of the wild-card game at the Vet. When a Rams reporter asked Buddy about the challenge of defending Greg Bell, who had rushed for 1,137 yards with 15 touchdowns that year, Ryan gave a bland answer about what a good back Bell was, then as he walked toward the back of the room past where we were all sitting, he muttered to the beat guys, “Greg Bell, my ass,” and cackled as he left the room. Bell rushed for 124 yards and a touchdown and also caught a 23-yard pass in the Rams’ 21-7 win. To this day Bell’s 147 scrimmage yards are 3rd-most by an opposing player in a playoff game in Philadelphia. Typical Buddy. Funny but ultimately empty bluster.

item.title: Eagles turning to Dontayvion Wicks and others without DeVonta Smith
item.description: Without DeVonta Smith in Week 4, the Eagles will be relying on their other receivers, starting with Dontayvion Wicks.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles turning to Dontayvion Wicks and others without DeVonta Smith originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Through three weeks of the 2026 season, Dontayvion Wicks has proven that he can be a legitimate WR2 in the NFL.

Time to see if he can be a WR1.

Because the Eagles won’t have DeVonta Smith (hamstring) when they face the Rams on Sunday afternoon, Wicks will take over as the team’s top receiver in Week 4 and perhaps longer.

“We’re prepared. It’s next man up,” Wicks said this week. “When you get to practice and get the reps in with the other guys out there, we’re ready for everybody to step up. You know, it’s football. You that those times show up, come up during seasons. It’s a long season. So some weeks you might not have guys out there. But we’re just going with it and however it play out, we’re going to be ready.”

Without Smith (hamstring) and Hollywood Brown (ankle), the Eagles receivers on Sunday will be Wicks, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Elijah Moore and Britain Covey. They’ll need contributions from most of them, but it really starts with Wicks.

The Eagles’ coaching staff was extremely impressed by how good Wicks looked in his role as the top receiver this week in practice. The Eagles have been high on Wicks since before he got to town and they still feel that way.

“He can do everything really,” Makai Lemon said of Wicks. “He’s one of the guys we count on in this offense. He can do everything.”

Through the first three weeks of the season, Smith has been featured in the Eagles’ offense at an extremely high rate. In fact, according to NFL NextGen Stats, Smith has the second-highest target share among all receivers in the NFL. Smith has seen 32.9% of the Eagles’ targets this year, which ranks behind just reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba at 37.9%.

So it’s obviously a big deal to not have Smith in a game against one of the top contenders in the NFC — a 1-2 Rams team that desperate for a win.

How do the Eagles game-plan without Smith?

“You go through it, and you think about the things that you do well and that your guys do well,” head coach Nick Sirainni said. “You think about the defense that you’re playing and the things that you have to do there and you put guys in positions — it’s, ‘OK, we’re running a play that Smitty might be good at and he’s the first reader,’ whatever it is. Then you say, ‘Hey, this play is still good and who’s the guy that should go in for that situation?’ 

“That’s kind of how it goes of when you’re getting ready for anything like that. You do that a lot. There’s guys that are questionable all week that you do that with and you have backup and contingency plans and all those different things. So again, it’s just part of our process of what we do on a weekly basis.”

For the previous four years, the Eagles had an incredible luxury at the receiver position with two legitimate No. 1s in A.J. Brown and Smith. When one of them missed time, at least they had the other. Maybe they don’t have that exact luxury anymore — but it’s worth noting again just how high the team has been on Wicks.

And it’s also worth noting that Jalen Hurts already seems to have a really high level of trust in Wicks after just three games.

Wicks so far has been targeted 15 times and has 9 catches for 179 yards and a touchdown. He’s second behind Smith in targets, catches and yards. It’s obviously early but the trade to bring Wicks in from Green Bay has looked very good.

In this game, the Eagles will likely play Wicks, Lemon and Cooper the most, but also expect Moore to rotate in. Lemon has already been playing a ton as the Eagles’ slot receiver but Cooper and Moore should see an uptick in their playing time.

“We feel like everyone’s capable of shouldering that burden,” offensive coordinator Sean Mannion said this week. “Wicks has been doing a ton of great stuff. Makai’s been doing a ton of great stuff. You look across the board at multiple different position groups. We feel confident in our depth across the board, and they’re going to step up to really help us continue to grow and improve as an offense.”

The production for Lemon hasn’t been great early in this season. The first-round pick from USC has just 7 catches for 38 yards, but it’s not his fault the team keeps trying to get him involved on ill-fated screens. When Lemon is asked to just run routes and catch the ball, he has looked fine.

If the Eagles are able to lean into his strengths, they should be able to unlock his ability more and more. That will need to start this week.

“Makai is nice,” Wicks said. “Results don’t always show up how everybody think they will so early. But he’s doing the right things, he’s stacking days. I see him every day get better every day. That’s a plus when you see that from a young guy. Remembering when I came in, the focal point was to stack days and get better every day. I see that from him. Him just gaining that confidence and also building that trust with 1, it’s big.”
